INTRODUCTION
The UEFA Technical Observer Group
provided comprehensive coverage
of the action as the UEFA Champions
League entered a new era in 2024/25
This review of the 2024/25 UEFA Champions League season covers
a campaign that featured a new format as the September-January
league phase replaced the September-December group stage. It
involved an additional four teams – up from 32 to 36 – and meant
that the overall number of matches rose to 189, the last of which
was the final at the Munich Football Arena on 31 May.
To assess the action, the UEFA Technical Observer Group worked
together with the UEFA performance analysis unit from September
through to May. An observer was assigned to analyse each fixture
from Matchday 1 onwards, with one present in the stadium for
every fixture in the knockout stage. Their insights have informed the
assessment of the tactical approach of each participating club as
well as the broader points addressed.

With the trends identified and explored, and the statistical
analysis provided, UEFA seeks to offer a meaningful resource to
coaches across Europe, offering information about today’s prevailing
styles and strategies and the qualities needed at the elite end of
European club football – as well as including coaching reflections for
those working on the development side of the game.

TRAINING GROUND TIPS
Pressing
“You need to have the right mentality to do this. The
individual is hugely important but football is still a team sport   they have an opportunity to play in different positions.
and everybody needs to play their part. As a coach you can
train your players so they’re physically ready to do this, but
the mentality depends on the individual.
“We educate players about this from a young age as part
of our development philosophy. We play a high press all the
time. We say, ‘We want to make you ready to play the most
difficult football’ and that means playing really high and
being ready at the back to play 1v1 to deal with that space.
This way we try to develop not only the mentality to press,
but also players who will be the very best in decision-making
on the defensive side, regarding positioning and 1v1s.
“Up to Under-14s, our players play 5v5 or 8v8. If it’s a 5v5
we say to the four outfield players, ‘Where is the ball?

Attack
the ball with two or three players.’ It’s already teaching them
in an unconscious way the principles of counter-pressing –
overload the ball area to win it back.”

RELENTLESS

SPIRIT
Luis Enrique talks about the improvements
both in attack and defence which were key
to his Paris Saint-Germain side becoming
champions of Europe

WI N NING COACH
“We have a trait that I think defines us, and that’s that
we always keep playing in the same way. Whether we’re
winning or losing, the result doesn’t affect us.” With
these words, Luis Enrique captures something of the
relentless spirit of his Paris Saint-Germain side, a group
of players whose unceasing intensity mirrors that of
their coach – and which was no better expressed than in
May’s Champions League final.
On that evening in Munich, Paris achieved the biggest
final winning margin in the competition’s history by
beating Inter 5-0. However, as Luis Enrique reflects,
it was an outcome he could not have dared to dream
of back in the winter, when they flirted with early
elimination after winning just one – and losing three
– of their first five games in the league phase. By the
season’s end, though, they had become the first French
club to complete a treble of Champions League, Ligue 1
and Coupe de France victories.

Here, the 55-year-old reflects on the thrilling run that
took them from that tentative start to their triumphant
finish, sealing a maiden Champions League title for his
club and a second for himself as a coach, ten years after
his first conquest of Europe with Barcelona.
If we look back to your team’s position after Matchday 5,
could you have imagined that you would win the
Champions League and make history by winning it
so decisively?
It would be very difficult go that far because,
normally, elite football is played based on the current
mood, and the time you’re talking about was a very
precarious one when the objective was to advance
to the next round – to advance as one of the top 24,
not to win the Champions League. So, I’d have to
say that, at that very precarious time, it would have
been practically impossible. I have to be honest.

But
I think this Champions League produced something
really wonderful for us because we went from being
practically ruled out to having a real chance of winning
the Champions League. The team grew over time and
overcame those situations and improved, especially in
terms of goalscoring, and in the end, the icing on the
cake was the final against Inter.

do you explain the way the team grew in maturity and
confidence from January onwards?
I think the precarious moment, above all, came from
that special tension and that lack of effectiveness in
the opening games of the Champions League. It’s a
short competition with this new format – eight games
to begin with. In the first three or four games, we were
walking a tightrope, but I think we deserved to get
many more points. We didn’t get them and things
started to get hairy, so our confidence dropped. When

we wouldn’t be overwhelmed by the setting or the
moment of the game, because we were surrounded
– as you would expect – by fans keen to support us,
trying to give us energy. You know, when there is too
much of anything, it’s a bad thing. We already knew we

Of course, [but] having lots of star players play for

It was a moment that the
Paris Saint-Germain fans and the club itself had been

How do you sum up the moment of victory as a
Champions League-winning coach?
What engulfs you over those days is extreme tension,
with everyone hoping to have that opportunity
Inter, who had been in a final two years earlier. It’s a
moment that has now gone down in history: beautiful
memories, beautiful images, many moments and a lot
of suffering, which is ultimately what makes you value
things. When you have suffered, you treasure those
moments of happiness, and in that sense I think it was
the perfect season.
Finally, after such an exceptional season, what targets
have you set for the next campaign?
The aim for this upcoming season is to improve. In
terms of titles, it’s going to be harder because there are
more titles to play for. But, in footballing terms, I think
we’ll improve as a team, both in attack and defence.
I believe we can still identify phases of the game to
get better in. In terms of titles, we want to be ready
to go for all of them.

Of course, we all believe we can
win them all and repeat this feat again this year, which
would mean going down in history in true fashion, and
that gives us special motivation.

ANALYSIS
Close study of individual matches over
the course of the season helped the UEFA
Technical Observer Group build up a clear
picture of the main trends and talking points
from a campaign that entered new territory

ROA D T O M U NICH
The 2024/25 UEFA Champions League commenced with the competition’s inaugural league phase,
which ran between 17 September and 29 January. This was a departure from the long-established
group-stage concept first introduced in 1991/92 and it meant that, rather than a cluster of four-team
groups, there was instead a single 36-team league in which each side played eight matches – four
home and four away. Overall, 144 games were played and 16 national associations were represented
though, amid the novelties, a familiar face finished top in the form of a Liverpool side victorious in
their first seven matches. Another change was the play-off round that followed in the new year, prior
to the round of 16, and with more games there was no shortage of talking points for UEFA’s Technical
Observer Group – as reflected in the following section-by-section analysis of this season’s competition.
LEAGUE PHASE

BUILDING FROM THE BACK
Players in different positions have a significant role
in constructing play, starting with the goalkeepers

MAIGNAN'S CALM DISTRIBUTION
When it comes to teams building from the back, the
goalkeeper will invariably be the first player under the   “You have to practise it throughout the week. You
microscope – and one custodian who stood out during
the league phase was Mike Maignan of AC Milan.
The Frenchman’s display in the 3-1 victory at Real
Madrid gave a strong example of how a goalkeeper
can help his team achieve good variations in their
build-up. “Maignan was key as he was so calm and
secure when building up,” said UEFA Technical
Observer Ole Gunnar Solskjær, who cited how Milan
had a “slow and controlled build-up when they
wanted and then quick transitions when they felt
there was an end product”.
Maignan caught the eye throughout with his
composure, never looking stressed by Madrid’s press.
Moreover, his excellent use of the ball meant he was
able to launch a range of deliveries from deep.

Barcelona’s bold high line against Inter raised the

GAME OF RISK AT SAN SIRO
As the excitement subsided following Inter’s 4-3 semi-final
second-leg success against Barcelona, a key tactical theme
stood out for further analysis: the visitors’ high back line
and how Inter sought to exploit the space behind it.
The bottom illustration of Barcelona’s back line without
the ball shows that the deepest visiting defender was,
on average, 40.8m from his own goal.
According to Coach Educator Phil Church, a high
defensive line has three main benefits: Reducing the
space and time the opposition have to play in, reducing
passing options for the opposition and allowing you to
get multiple players and pressure on the ball quickly to
regain it and control the game.
There is the additional advantage that the opposition
have more distance to travel if they do get behind, giving
more time for players to recover. That said, the strategy
demands an aggressive mindset and confidence given
the space left behind.

HOW TO BEAT A HIGH LINE
To beat a high line, players must recognise spaces between
defenders and pass with speed and accuracy. Teams need to
deploy fast attackers who play high on the defensive line and can
break behind. Players must be brave to play quickly in tight areas
with the opposition squeezing space.

WHERE THE GOALS WERE SCORED
As the location map (bottom) illustrates, a significant majority of
goals in the 2024/25 campaign were scored inside the penalty box –
89% of the total.
Barcelona and Paris Saint-Germain led the way, with 33 goals
inside the box each, followed by Bayern (30). The most goals from
outside the box came from Barcelona too (seven), with Arsenal
scoring six.
As for shooting attempts overall, Paris recorded the most (319),
though Bayern had more shots per 90 minutes on average – 20.2
to Paris’s 18.8.
First-touch finishing
Three of the five goals in the final came from first-touch finishes
and this was the most popular way to score overall, accounting for
56% of goals. Paris Saint-Germain scored 17 times through first-
touch strikes – more than any other club. Inter (14), Arsenal (13) and
Barcelona (12) were next.
To break down the scoring further, 52% of goals were right-foot
finishes, with 36% coming from left-foot shots and 12% from
headers.

Among the 36 participating teams, eight bucked the
trend with a majority share of left-foot goals: Barcelona, Arsenal,
Manchester City, Bayer Leverkusen, GNK Dinamo, Slovan Bratislava,
Sparta Praha and Salzburg.

GOAL KICKS
This section explores how restarts were used to progress the ball,
manipulate pressing structures and create space – with standout
examples from Lille, Manchester City and Bayern München. An
analysis of the total of 2,581 goal kicks across the campaign found
that almost one quarter (24%) were taken by an outfield player.
Starting goal kicks with a centre-back rather than the goalkeeper
has become increasingly common and was observed frequently during
this season’s UEFA Champions League. When the centre-back initiates
play, opponents typically respond by locking on to nearby outfield
options to prepare a pressing trap, rather than directly applying
pressure on the goalkeeper, who is typically positioned centrally.
Pressing the goalkeeper centrally may allow space to an outfield player
instead and with it comes the risk of being exposed behind the first
line of pressure. For the side building play, meanwhile, it allows the
keeper more time on the ball and is a strategy that can be helpful for
coping with player-to-player pressure.

Of all the clubs competing from the league phase onwards, Lille
had the highest percentage of goal kicks taken by outfield players
(53%), with left-sided centre-back Alexsandro taking more than
goalkeeper Lucas Chevalier (42 to 38), as illustrated by the image
below, taken from their visit to Liverpool. In this example, Alexsandro
played the ball to his full-back, rather than goalkeeper, and Lille
retained the ball at the back before a longer pass forward to exploit
space behind.

HIGH PRESS
Arsenal were the team that had the most success in preventing
their opponents from passing out of the defensive third, stopping
two fifths (42%) of opposition passes from the defensive to mid or
attacking thirds. This is shown in the graphics to the right, with the
second chart highlighting that the English side stopped an average
of 22.2 opposition passes out of the defensive third per game.
The game in which Arsenal disrupted their opponents’ build-up the
most was the semi-final second leg at Paris Saint-Germain, where
they stopped 60% of their hosts’ passes out of the defensive third –
which was 20% above their tournament average. This is all the more
impressive considering that the eventual champions completed 69%
of all passes out of the defensive third across the campaign.
A key feature for Arsenal was their front players applying pressure,
with the centre-backs behind the ball willing to step in to intercept
opposition passes through the lines.

Mikel Arteta’s men had already caused Paris Saint-Germain
problems with the intensity of their high pressing when the teams
met on Matchday 2 in London and Arsenal prevailed 2-0. Luis Enrique,
the Paris coach, admitted that night that Arsenal “pressed us high
from the first minute and we couldn’t overcome it”.
The image below captures a moment in the game when Arsenal,
from a compact mid-block shape, took the opportunity to force Paris
backwards, with their forward players and winger Bukayo Saka leading
the press and centre-back William Saliba and right-back Jurriën
Timber then joining in. Saliba’s aggressive movement upfield to get
tight to João Neves is highlighted. As UEFA Technical Observer Rafa
Benítez observed: “The timing and understanding of when to press all
together was very clear.”

GOALKEEPING
The UEFA Goalkeeper Expert Group analyse
four key themes from the 2024/25 campaign
Building play, defending corners, making saves and preventing
chances all went under the microscope when the UEFA Goalkeeper
Expert Group, headed by Frans Hoek and Mart Poom, analysed the
2024/25 season from a goalkeeping perspective, with a study of the
13 matches from the quarter-finals onwards.

ROLE IN THE BUILD-UP
The first theme explored was the role of the goalkeeper in
possession-based play. Overall, the goalkeepers of all eight quarter-
final sides were involved in the build-up and for Hoek and Poom,
the overall standard has risen over the years in terms of reading the
game, decision-making and execution. “Goalkeepers are really part
of the team and, for many teams, a very important part, especially

A question of positioning
Another challenge for goalkeepers at this level comes from the
trend for so-called ‘wrong-footed’ wingers or wide attackers such
as Lamine Yamal and Mohamed Salah. When they come inside and
shoot with their stronger foot, it can be difficult for goalkeepers as   close distance – either box-side crosses or narrow crosses from near
the goal opens up for the forward and often there are bodies in the
box blocking the view.
For the UEFA Goalkeeper Expert Group, this raises the question
of whether a deeper position would be better for the goalkeeper, to
provide more time to see the ball and make the required adjustment
before diving. An example of such positioning came from Inter
goalkeeper Sommer in the second leg of the semi-final against
Barcelona, when he twice foiled Yamal in such situations.

shot towards the top corner from outside the box. Sommer, from a

and executed a flying save to his right.

save, shown in the bottom image, when Yamal cut in to curl the
ball towards the far post from the angle. In these situations, the
collaboration between the goalkeeper and his defenders is crucial

block the near-post area with his legs, meaning the goalkeeper can

The final theme is how goalkeepers dealt with high and low crosses,
cutbacks and other dangerous open-play balls. Frans Hoek and Mart
Poom said: “A lot of crosses at the elite level are now played from
the corner of the 16m box. As they are more precise, there is less
time for defenders or goalkeepers to intervene. Also, teams are
deliberately attacking the half-spaces and byline to make cutbacks.”
The chart below shows that crosses in the UEFA Champions
League (from quarter-finals to final) tended to be closer to the goal
than in the UEFA Europa League and UEFA Conference League.
Given the fact they were mostly low deliveries struck with good
quality and pace, the tendency from a lot of goalkeepers was to
leave them for their defenders and to concentrate more on the next
phase of defending the goal – as well as to be ready for any potential
loose balls that could result from a deflection, tackle or the like.

Distances covered and high-speed runs completed form the

both were impacted by players’ positions and team playing style
How much distance does a UEFA Champions League footballer cover
per match? And how much does that distance vary according to
their position? The table (top right) illustrates positional physical
output, with the pivot/No6 covering the highest total distance on
average (11.33 km) and forwards the lowest (9.96 km).
Although time spent in the higher-speed zones accounts for a
small proportion of the overall distance covered (approximately
8–10% of total distance depending on position), high-speed
running (SZ4 and SZ5) is often associated with defining moments
such as goalscoring opportunities or key defensive actions.
Wide players did the most high-speed running per game,
with an average distance covered of 1.04 km. These differences
between positions highlight the need to ensure that players are
prepared for their role, not just from a tactical perspective but also
in terms of the physical demands.

The study also found that the match-to-match variability in
total distance covered was relatively low (8–14% dependent on
position) in comparison to the variability in sprinting (39–49%
dependent on position). That variation in high-speed output
can be down to factors such as position, tactical strategies and
scoreline. It is also worth noting that there was no significant

SPOTLIGHT ON SPRINTS
In their analysis of 2024/25, the UEFA Fitness Group found that, on
average, forwards, full-backs and wide players completed the highest
number of sprints per game (between 19 and 22). There was no
difference between starters and substitutes, meanwhile, relative to
their output per minute.
As mentioned at the start of the analysis, a sprint is defined as
a high-speed run exceeding 25 km/h. More than half of the sprints
(55%) performed during the 2-24/25 season were sustained for
between 0 and 10 m. Interestingly, only 5% were between 30–40 m
and only 3% were greater than 40 m. These longer sprints typically
occur during transitional moments.

INTRODUCTION
The UEFA Technical Observer Group were
watching on throughout another engrossing
campaign to analyse the key tactical
trends and individual achievements
The 2024/25 UEFA Women’s Champions League report provides in-depth analysis and
key discussion points focusing on the technical and tactical trends from this season’s
competition.
Matches from the group stage through to the final in Lisbon on 24 May have been
analysed by UEFA’s Technical Observer Group. This process, which utilises UEFA’s
latest technological innovations, has prompted a wealth of fascinating insight and
discussion summarised in this report.
This year’s competition has further highlighted the continued evolution of elite
women’s football across Europe. Many teams and individuals have contributed to a
thoroughly engaging competition, which has been notable for numerous excellent
attacking performances as well as some standout defensive displays. A number of
these impressive individual performances have been captured in our comprehensive
awards section covering Team of the Season, Player of the Season, Young Player of the
Season and Top Scorer. The top ten goals of the competition are also listed.

This report celebrates both the players and the coaches, recognising their respective
contributions to the competition. We have seen many well-executed tactical setups,
as well as intelligent in-game management which are highlighted and discussed
through our round-by-round summaries as well as in-depth analysis sections.
Finally, we hope that the findings presented will help educate, engage and inspire all   Martin Sjögren (SWE)
those who work in coaching, coach education and young player development across
Europe and beyond.

FI NA L ANALY S IS

DOUBLE CHANGE TURNS THE TIDE
Arsenal’s 1-0 victory over Barcelona in the final of the
2024/25 UEFA Women’s Champions League owed much
to the introduction of second-half substitutes Stina
Blackstenius and Beth Mead. With the game locked
at 0-0 and Barcelona increasingly building attacking
momentum, Arsenal coach Renée Slegers made a
decisive double change that would shift the rhythm of the
game and give the north London side their first European
trophy in 18 years.
With 67 minutes played, Slegers withdrew forwards
Frida Maanum and Chloe Kelly, introducing Blackstenius
and Mead from the bench. The changes triggered a small
tactical adjustment that would prove crucial in deciding
who would lift the trophy in Lisbon. As part of the
reshuffle, Arsenal centre-forward Alessia Russo, who had
worked tirelessly at the top of the pitch, dropped into the
deeper position previously occupied by Maanum. With
Russo now looking to connect the game from a more
withdrawn position, Blackstenius was free to work up
against Barcelona’s back line.

“When Stina came into the game, she stretched the
game a lot more,” explained Gemma Grainger, UEFA
Technical Observer. “It meant Barcelona’s defenders had
to be aware of this threat in behind the back line and
moved their positioning a little bit deeper. She stretched
the game.
“Her ability to threaten behind Barcelona continued
to impact the game,” added Grainger. “It helped Arsenal
move up the pitch and gain territory in the opposition’s
half. Arsenal were able to win possession higher up the
pitch and started to win free-kicks in Barcelona’s half. It
meant Barcelona found it difficult to find their rhythm
and get momentum back, which was vital towards the
end of the game.”

IMPACT FROM THE BENCH
Following her arrival into the game, it took just seven
minutes for Blackstenius to score Arsenal’s decisive goal,
a crucial contribution that led to the Swedish forward
being named Player of the Match. “She had two chances
before the goal with her runs in behind, stretching the
game more,” explained Grainger. “Then came the goal,
showing her match-winning influence; Mead’s assist
also shows the impact of substitutions for Arsenal in
changing the game.”
Although Blackstenius will be hailed as Arsenal’s
game-changing substitute, the impact of Mead should
not be underestimated. “Mead also played a big role
when she came on,” explained Grainger. “She offered
different qualities to Chloe Kelly – playing more passes,
as opposed to running with the ball. This complemented
the runs that Blackstenius was making.
“The assist for the winning goal showed Mead’s
quality,” added Grainger. “She saw the movement of
the attacker and knew exactly where to play the pass.

DEFENSIVE DOMINANCE

PROVIDES PLATFORM
In addition to their clever use of substitutes, Arsenal’s
victory over Barcelona was built on a solid defensive
platform featuring excellence in both individual and
collective defending. A key part of the English side’s
defensive strategy was how they adopted different
pressing strategies including a high press, mid and low
defensive block based on Barcelona’s play. “Whether
Arsenal were pressing high, dropping deep or forcing
outside or inside, what was key was the distance
between the individuals and units,” explained
Anna Signeul, UEFA Technical Observer. “There was
excellent communication and organisation which
meant they did not leave any gaps which prevented
Barcelona from playing the ball forward in key areas.
“There was also a real discipline to the way they
defended,” added Signeul. “Arsenal were aware
of what Barcelona wanted to do and then stayed
together and worked so hard to defend against it.
The hard work they put in was very impressive.”

wanted to attack and making important interceptions.

WI N NING COACH
Looking back on the season, what were some of the
games that jumped out at you as the biggest challenges?
Different games have different challenges, and I
think what’s been so good about this team is that
we’ve wanted to overcome those challenges. There
are a couple of key moments. Of course, the Bayern
München game at home, because I think that’s when
we started to show how we wanted to try and get wins
over the line. [Regarding] Lyon, I think we spoke about
not knowing how we’re going to do against these
teams. But what the players also said after the first 30
minutes in the home game against them helped us
understand that we can compete with these teams.
We can do it. And I think the learning for the future
would be to do it from minute one, because we know
we can believe in ourselves.

And I think the speed of
the progress we’ve made, then being able to apply that
in the away leg with a lot of pressure on us and winning
4-1 [says a lot].
How would you like this team’s achievement to be
remembered in this season’s Champions League?
Not as a one-time thing because that’s obviously the
risk. I think we’ve been winning cups the last couple
of seasons, but there’s always been more wonderful
things to achieve. And now that we’ve won the
Champions League; it’s the ultimate thing to be the
champions of Europe. We did that in a very long run
of games with a lot of setbacks and not an easy start,
and we got the 1-0 win against Barcelona. We want to
be consistently high-performing, consistently winning
trophies, but we know how hard it is, so we’re very
humble and respectful about it. That’s the direction
we want to go in. If it’s a one-time thing, it’s still a
beautiful thing because of what the team achieved in
this tournament from start to finish.

Considering that we’ve spoken a lot about your
tactical approach and how you wanted your team
to play last season, what qualities and skills do your
players need to implement and execute this?
We demand so much from our players. We see
it when new players come in: we train at a really
high level. There’s a lot of detail we demand from
the players from a technical perspective. Every
touch, every pass – there needs to be detail on
it. Technical excellence is very important in the
style of play for Arsenal. We see that the game is
growing, and it’s growing fast, and physical qualities
are more and more important, so you need to be
very athletic to play our game. You see the players,
well in the end, you’ll see they need everything,
because I think we are operating at the highest
level. But you need resilience, you need a growth
mindset, you need to be a team player. Just a really
good basic understanding of football and how to
collaborate with players on the pitch.

Afterwards,
we obviously had some difficulties in the knockout
stages, as always. I suppose you could say it was
an uneven but well-executed Champions League
season for us.

Finally, who have been the biggest influences on your
coaching career? What do you think you’ve learnt from
them, and how do you apply it into your own work?
From a football context, it’s Martin Sjögren, a Swedish
coach that I had when I was a player, who’s now coaching
Hammarby. He contextualised football actions on the
pitch, so I started to understand more about tactics
and how one action affects the next. I grew up in the
Netherlands, with direction from coaches, instructions,
screaming and raised voices. Then I came to Sweden and
Martin was my coach. He was so calm. He would just say
in a calm tone what we were going to do, and what we
were going to change. He just made everything so clear.
And then Sarina Wiegman is a big inspiration for me, and
I’m so happy for her and what she achieved at the EURO.
She’s been an important pioneer in the Netherlands for
female coaching.

Everything she’s been fighting for –
getting the coaching badges, the courses – it wasn’t easy
back then as a woman, but she fought her way through
and she opened the gate for many others. But also in
the way she leads, and who she is as a person, there’s so
much inspiration for me. She’s very compassionate, but
she’s also very hard in her decision-making, so I think it’s
a very impressive balance.

GROUP STAGE
The 2024/25 UEFA Women’s Champions League marked the final edition of the group stage in its current format,
bringing together some of European football’s biggest names as well as a number of competition debutants.
Holders Barcelona were joined in the group stage by fellow former champions Arsenal, Lyon and Wolfsburg while
Galatasaray and Hammarby made their competition debuts.
Celtic, Manchester City, Twente and Vålerenga appeared in the group stage for the first time. Group A saw
Lyon and Wolfsburg pitted against each other, while Group C had Bayern, Arsenal and Juventus all vying for
a place in the quarter-finals. The 2025/26 UEFA Women’s Champions League will be the first season under a
new format with an expanded entry and an 18-team league phase replacing the old group stage, mirroring the
updated formats of the UEFA men’s club competitions. This review of the group stage studies eight matches and
the tactical themes that underpinned them.

BAYERN v ARSENAL

PLAY THROUGH THE PRESS

2024/25 Women’s Champions League campaign with a
5-2 win over Arsenal on Matchday 1. Building from the back
was integral to this display from Alexander Straus’ team,
who demonstrated their intent to play through the thirds
of the pitch during what was a comprehensive victory.
Deep-lying midfielder Georgia Stanway, operating
as one of two Bayern midfield pivots, played a central

international routinely moved away from central areas to
a wider position behind Arsenal’s two central attackers as

movement was twofold: either she found space to receive
and start an attack from a wide position, or she tempted

cleverly found ways to play through Arsenal’s press.

If the final score was disappointing for Arsenal,

CELTIC FORCED TO PLAY LONG
Chelsea’s effective high-press strategy provided the
platform for their narrow 2-1 away victory over Celtic on
Matchday 3. With the Scottish outfit eager to play short
from the back, Sonia Bompastor’s troops implemented
an aggressive 1v1 press with pressure applied to Celtic’s
back line, including goalkeeper Kelsey Daugherty.
The fact that the hosts were looking to build through
their goalkeeper and two centre-backs prompted

to apply pressure to Celtic’s key players in the build-up.

VÅLERENGA v BAYERN

UNITY AND DISCIPLINE
Vålerenga’s standout performance in the group
stage came on Matchday 4 with a 1-1 draw against
Bayern. Using a low-block defensive approach, the
Norwegian club produced a disciplined defensive
display that was rewarded with a point against their
German visitors.
With four midfield screening players stationed in
front of a back line of five defenders, Vålerenga’s
strategy was to reduce the spaces for Bayern to
penetrate centrally. To do so, the home side had to
be coordinated in their movements and individually
disciplined in their 1v1 duels with opponents.
By shuffling and sliding across the pitch in
unison, Vålerenga’s defensive template was rarely
broken with Nils Lexerød’s team maintaining the
distances between their defensive units for large
parts of the match.
Communication was key to implementing
the strategy, with Vålerenga’s players effective
in passing players on during Bayern’s positional
rotation, as well as being quick to double up in wide
areas. The hosts’ excellent defensive showing was
emphasised by Bayern posting their lowest xG of the
group stage at just 1.33.

ARSENAL v REAL MADRID

TIMING AND TECHNIQUE TO THE FORE
Arsenal reached the semi-finals after two second-leg
goals from Alessia Russo helped her side overcome a
2-0 first-leg deficit and record a 3-2 aggregate victory
over Real Madrid.
Both of Russo’s goals were a product of first-time
finishes and showcased the striker’s technical prowess
around the penalty box. “Russo was getting into the
five-metre box, into the positions to score with a
first-time finish,” Gemma Grainger elaborated. “The
technical ability and execution of this type of strike is
very complex. Russo just makes it look very good and
very easy. She took both goals early – it’s a very complex
technical execution. She is technically efficient.”
For Arsenal’s opener, Russo benefited from an early
cross from Chloe Kelly on the right. With Madrid’s
defenders running back towards their own goal – and
not yet in an optimal defensive position – Russo was
able to exploit the space between the back line and
goalkeeper to effect her first-time finish.

Importantly,
the Arsenal attacker had stayed onside by remaining
patient and making small adjustments in her position
to ensure she kept in line with the last defender.
“Russo’s timing to arrive as the ball arrives was crucial,”
added Grainger.
“No9s should have more than one movement to
arrive out of the eyeline of the defender and be able to
move across or behind their marker to react. Attackers
may have to make three movements in the penalty
area in order to find the space to score. This gives
the crosser some clear areas to target and options to
play to different players. It also makes it difficult to
defend.”
For Arsenal’s third goal, Russo made a clever curved
run into the centre of the penalty area as the free-
kick from the right was delivered. Although Arsenal’s
No23 didn’t receive the initial delivery, she stayed alert
and so anticipated where the knockdown would land,
producing a clever finish inside the penalty box.
“Attackers need good balance to finish first-time
in the penalty area,” added Grainger.

“Often these
are awkward finishes where the attacker may have to
adjust and may be in contact with the defender. This
makes it harder, for the technical execution, to finish.”

SEMI-FINALS
Barcelona and Arsenal progressed to the UEFA Women’s Champions League final in Lisbon after impressive
semi-final victories over Chelsea and Lyon respectively. Barcelona’s 8-2 aggregate success meant the Catalans

standout result and 5-3 aggregate triumph.

Semi-final first leg: Arsenal 1-2 Lyon
Lyon seized the initiative in their semi-final against
Arsenal after goals from Kadidiatou Diani and Melchie
Dumornay secured the 2024 runners-up a 2-1 first-leg
victory in London.
Lyon blended forward flair and defensive resilience
to claim the spoils. Joe Montemurro’s team went
ahead after 17 minutes when Diani capped off a
clever build-up move. However, Arsenal looked to have
earned a draw as Mariona Caldentey equalised with a
penalty in the 78th minute, only for Dumornay to hit
the winner four minutes later.

YOUNG PLAYER OF THE SEASON

MELCHIE DUMORNAY
The forward scored six goals and set up two more in her
breakthrough campaign as Lyon reached the last four
Melchie Dumornay produced a number of impressive performances
as her Lyon side reached the semi-finals. The 22-year-old Haiti
international displayed her many attacking talents including powerful
running with and without the ball, excellent technique as well as
positional rotation and game understanding.
One of her standout performances came in a 2-0 victory over
Bayern München in the quarter-final first leg. “When Dumornay was
playing with her back to the opponent she was very tough to defend,”
explained Fritzy Kromp, UEFA Technical Observer. “The Bayern
defenders had no chance to get the ball or see the ball.”
Dumornay’s willingness to drop into deeper positions to receive
and play forward also caused numerous problems for Bayern and
was the key feature of Lyon’s attacking play. “It was outstanding
how much she was dropping in different spaces,” added Kromp.

“She would regularly come deeper than the holding midfielder to
receive and once she had the game in front of her, she was even
tougher to defend.
“It was really remarkable to see how her movement worked with
her team-mates. When she was dropping into midfield in a very
low position, a midfield player would then move into the forward
position. It looked very familiar to all of the players and they knew
what to do when Dumornay moved into midfield. It was a very good
team performance.”
Dumornay was also influential in the French side’s first-leg victory
at Arsenal in the semi-finals. "She was a constant threat in possession
with her movement between the lines and her ability to run behind at
pace,” explained Jayne Ludlow, UEFA Technical Observer. “There was
a strong rotational understanding in the front three and good timing
of movement for combinations at speed. Her aggressive pressing was
part of Lyon's front line and it was a great clinical finish for her goal.”

PINA TOP FOR GOAL CONTRIBUTIONS
As well as finishing top of the scoring table for the 2024/25 UEFA
Women’s Champions League, Pina also led the way with the highest
number of goals and assists combined. She added an assist to her
total of ten goals to finish with a combined total of 11. The attacker’s
position at the top of the goals and assists table underlines her wide-
ranging contribution to Barcelona’s attack. As well as proving adept at
finishing Pina, who often drifts in from the left of the attack,
is unselfish in her approach to creating chances for others.
On a similar note, Player of the Season Aitana Bonmatí added five
assists to her four goals for an overall score of nine in the combined
goals and assists list.

WIDE PLAYERS MAKE THEIR MARK
Wide attackers were the most prolific scorers in the competition,
registering 69 goals, one more than centre-forwards. That closeness
in numbers highlights both the evolving role of the wide player and
the centre-forward as well as the fluidity of attacking movement
adopted by many of the competition’s best teams.
Lyon’s Kadidiatou Diani, Melchie Dumornay and Tabitha Chawinga,
who scored 14 goals between them, were one example of a forward
line who regularly interchanged positions. As a result, it was often
the wide players who moved inside into central goalscoring areas.
“We've worked a lot on it at training,” explained Lyon head coach
Joe Montemurro. “If they stay in position, it's a lot easier to read
so they are the ones in the moment to identify the space. One will
come short and take a defender away, another one will go over the
top or come inside. So they have this autonomy and effectively they
understand where the space is in the moments.”

Attacking in this way requires a coordinated approach and the
ability to read the movements of team-mates, explains Jayne
Ludlow, UEFA Technical Observer. “Coaches should look at the timing
of the movement and how the attackers read the movement of
each other,” explains Ludlow. “The attackers have to be very reactive
to the movement of their team-mates. The movement of your
team-mate is the trigger for you to make a different movement and
that is how they make their decisions.”

BUILD-UP PHASE
WILLIAMSON GOAL KICKS

KEY FOR ARSENAL
Goal kicks taken by central defender Leah Williamson were a key
feature of Arsenal’s build-up play in the final against Barcelona. The
England captain regularly initiated play from goal kicks, either passing
short to goalkeeper Daphne van Domselaar or playing further forward
into Arsenal’s front line.
With Barcelona intent on pressing high from Arsenal’s goal kicks,
Williamson’s variety kept their opponents guessing as to where
the next pass would be delivered. If Williamson played short to her
goalkeeper, Barcelona’s attackers were unsure whether to press and
leave the two centre-backs. Similarly, by encouraging the opposition
to press high, Williamson also had the option to play over the high
press and directly into the front line.
How Arsenal varied their build-up play in the final was a
key feature of Renée Slegers’ side’s approach.

“With Arsenal bringing two
midfielders down when they had a goal kick, and the full-backs trying to
drag Barcelona down as well, they were able to attract pressure high up
the pitch and pin Barcelona’s back line in 1v1 situations on the halfway
line,” explained Tanya Oxtoby, UEFA Technical Observer. “Often, they
played over the press into the front line. That was really intelligent as
Barcelona didn’t have the chance to press them high up the pitch, which
is what they wanted to do. Even when Arsenal were not successful, they
were able to pick up second balls and relieve a little bit of pressure.”
When playing into their forwards Arsenal tried to create overloads
in wide areas to gain a further advantage. “They were clearly trying
to go into either Alessia Russo or Caitlin Foord on the left, so they
were overloading one side of the pitch, which was interesting,” added
Oxtoby. “They had a really clear strategy and thought through how they
were going to limit any damage Barcelona could do in their high press.

Because Barcelona like to be aggressive and on the front foot it caused
them a number of problems. They struggled to press high and get the
balance right behind the ball. It was a really interesting tactical battle.”
Arsenal’s approach to taking goal kicks was consistent throughout
the competition with the English side registering the most goal kicks
from an outfield player. Arsenal were not the only team that adopted
the approach of outfield players initiating goal kicks. Of the 937 goal
kicks taken in the competition, 26% were taken by outfield players.
The average length of the first pass from a goal kick was 23.4 metres.

FINISHING THE ATTACK

EARLY CROSSES CAUSES DISRUPTION
Arsenal’s 3-0 victory over Real Madrid in the quarter-final second leg
highlighted the effectiveness of crosses. Trailing 2-0 from the first
leg, the London side produced an impressive demonstration of wide
deliveries in the second half to record a 3-2 aggregate victory.
Following a first half in which Arsenal enjoyed most of the possession
and created numerous crossing opportunities, there was a subtle
change in attacking approach after the restart. Arsenal started the
second period by delivering a number of early crosses into the Madrid
penalty box. With right-winger Chloe Kelly demonstrating her ability to
deliver first-time crosses, Arsenal looked to exploit the space between
Madrid’s retreating defence and the goalkeeper.
“Chloe Kelly’s early deliveries in the second half meant that Real
Madrid were less organised in the box,” explained Gemma Grainger,
UEFA Technical Observer. “Early crosses are difficult for the defending
team because there is limited reaction time. Also, in these situations,
defenders are usually running back towards their own goal.

If the cross
is delivered under head high and the defender is facing their own goal it
can be dangerous from a defensive perspective.”
Arsenal looked to create 1v1 situations for Kelly in wide areas and
the England winger had the technical quality to execute the delivery.
“A really big consideration for all coaches is playing players in their most
effective positions to utilise their strengths,” explains Grainger. “How a
coach gives players the opportunity to deliver their strengths in a game
as well as exploit the opposition through a game plan all links together.
The game plan and the player strengths are two very important parts
of a coach’s thinking. Ultimately, teams at the highest level are more
organised defensively. What we saw with Kelly is that the early delivery
meant Real Madrid were less organised in the box. She was the player
who could deliver the cross with that technical ability and that links
back to create a game plan for a player’s individual strengths.”

Lyon’s ability to regain the ball in the attacking third was a key

The French side used the physical qualities of Dumornay and
Lindsey Heaps to support attacker Ada Hegerberg in applying
pressure to the opposition back line.

looked to split the centre-backs when they built from the back and
Dumornay and Heaps would break out from their deeper position

controlled the space in front of the back line.”
Heaps, alongside fellow midfielder Egurrola, impressed
throughout the competition for their understanding of when to
step forward and press and when to stay and screen forward passes.
“They were making constant adjustments as the ball moved,”
explained Jayne Ludlow, UEFA Technical Observer. “They were also
reading the triggers of the opposition in order to get the timing of

penetrating was a standout feature of their run to the quarter-
finals. Overall 44% of the English side’s ball recoveries occurred in
the middle third, averaging 27 mid-block regains per game. Their
efficiency in this aspect of the game was underlined during their
group stage fixture against St. Pölten, when they recorded 42 mid-
block regains – the highest of the season.
In total 36% of City’s mid-third regains came in central areas,
a figure matched only by Barcelona. Crucial to City’s work in this
area of the pitch was the contribution of Japanese international
midfielder Yui Hasegawa, who recorded the most mid-third ball
recoveries in the competition with 46. Given City played three
fewer games than finalists Arsenal and Barcelona, Hasegawa’s work
in this area was significant.
In the clips Hasegawa demonstrates the importance of
awareness, anticipation and speed of movement when
intercepting passes.

midfielder can be seen checking for the movement of her
opponents, while also predicting the weight, timing and angle
of pass from the ball carrier. Although diminutive in stature,
Hasegawa’s excellent anticipation skills allowed her to effectively
intercept passes without always having to enter physical 1v1
defensive duels.

ARSENAL FORCE OPPONENTS

WIDE TO REGAIN
Arsenal adopted a different approach to Manchester City when
attempting to recover the ball in the middle third of the pitch. Where
City looked to regain in central areas, Arsenal remained compact
with the aim of forcing their opposition wide. Just 29% of Renée
Slegers’s side’s mid-block regains came from the centre of the mid-
block, whereas 71% were made in wide areas.
“Arsenal worked so hard to stay compact and press the ball in
good positions,” explained Martin Sjögren, UEFA Technical Observer,
following their 4-1 victory over Lyon in the semi-final second leg.
“They have really good defensive structure and compactness. They
were on the front foot throughout the game and won a lot of duels.”
Arsenal regularly adopted a 4-4-2 shape in their mid-block with
important contributions from their two highest attacking players.
“Arsenal defended in a 4-4-2 mid-block with the aim of moving
out of the mid-block to a high press. They were compact and used
zonal defending,” explained Sjögren.

“The two highest attacking
players, Alessia Russo and Frida Maanum, were very good in their
collaboration to press and cover the space behind them. They put
in a lot of running to help the team and get a good start to the
defending phase.”
Crucial to Arsenal’s strategy of forcing play wide were the 1v1
defensive skills of their full-backs Emily Fox and Katie McCabe. In
particular right-back Fox proved crucial in regaining the ball when
forced into wide areas. The USA international was the only wide
player in the top five for mid-block regains with 29.
In the clips, Fox demonstrates her impressive reading of the game
and physical qualities, as well as her determination and technique
in 1v1 defensive duels. The full-back was deservedly selected in the
UEFA Women’s Champions League Team of the Season for 2024/25.

competition, underlining their commitment to a collective defensive
approach.

Chelsea first to make contact
Chelsea’s run to the semi-finals owed much to their solid central
defensive pairing of Nathalie Björn and Millie Bright. Chelsea’s
centre-backs were effective when defending crosses, registering
a combined total of 37% of their team’s first contacts.
The clip below highlights how both Björn and Bright adopted
optimal positions in the penalty area to make first contact on
crosses. When the ball moved wide, the Chelsea defenders quickly
adjusted their position to ensure they were stationed inside the
width of the goal giving themselves the best possible opportunity to
successfully defend against the delivery.
Much of Björn and Bright’s preparatory work was done before the
cross was delivered. Both defenders can be seen scanning for danger
inside the penalty box, as well as trying to read the cues of the
crossing player. By preparing early and adjusting their position, both
central defenders were able to attack the ball and make strong first
contacts.

Following a successful first contact, Chelsea’s defensive
pair were quick to move out of the penalty area, ensuring they
weren’t too deep if the ball was returned.
The work of Björn and Bright helped their side record the highest
percentage of first contacts when facing crosses (73%), limiting the
opposition to just 1.7 shots from crosses per game.

ATTACKING
TRANSITIONS

BARCELONA TURN REGAINS INTO SHOTS
Barcelona’s ability to regain the ball in the opposition’s half regularly
led to shots on target for the Spanish side. Pere Romeu’s team
registered the highest average number of shots from defensive
actions in the opposition half with six per game. Across the
competition, the losing finalists created 67 shots following defensive
actions in the opposition half.
“One of the key elements of Barcelona’s game was in moments
when they regained the ball,” explained Britta Carlson, UEFA
Technical Observer, following Barcelona’s 4-1 victory over Wolfsburg
in the quarter-final first leg. “They have the ability to
use combination and speed of play to transition effectively to final-
third areas and often look to transition within inside channels or
wide areas.”
Following regains in the final third, Barcelona’s individual technical
ability and coordinated attacking movement routinely led to shots
on target and goals, as demonstrated with their fifth in their 9-0
group stage victory over Hammarby.

“In attacking transitions in the final third, Barcelona looked for
over and underlapping movements to then attempt a penetrative
pass in behind the opponents,” added Carlson. “There was also good
use of supporting numbers behind the ball to continue momentum
of the transitional moment, as well as to make attacking numbers in
and around the box.”
The Spanish side also demonstrated their ability to vary their
approach to attacking transitions. When the ball was regained
in their own half they were willing to play forward early into their
highest attacking player or into the space beyond the back line.
“After winning the ball in their own half, the first pass was usually
played directly deep or diagonally to the outside attacking players
or the top player, often Ewa Pajor, for a deep pass or long pass
behind the back line,” explained Carlson. “There was also a different
approach when the ball was regained in the mid-block where they
tended to play for possession and ball protection.”
LYON LEAD THE WAY FROM

DEEP COUNTERATTACKS
Lyon’s ability to regain the ball in their own half and quickly
launch counterattacks proved an effective attacking strategy. The
French side created the most shots in the competition from deep
counterattacks, with 13 shots via this route to goal.
As demonstrated with their third goal against Bayern München
in the quarter-final second leg, the speed, movement and technical
ability of their forward players proved difficult for opposition teams
to contain.
“When Lyon’s front three of Kadidiatou Diani, Melchie Dumornay
and Tabitha Chawinga combine they are lethal, because they’ve
got pace, technique and their timing and movement are good,”
explained Jayne Ludlow, UEFA Technical Observer, following Lyon’s
2-1 victory at Arsenal in the semi-final first leg. “There is a strong
rotational understanding in the front three and good timing of
movement for combinations at speed.”
Coaches can help players develop coordinated attacking
transitions by encouraging individuals to read the movements
and cues of their team-mates.

“From a coaching perspective, it’s
about the detail of the first pass into the attacking players, then
it’s looking at the timing of the movement and how the attackers
read the movement of each other,” explains Ludlow. “The attackers
have to be very reactive to the movement of their team-mates.
The movement of your team-mate is the trigger for you to make a
different movement and that is how they make their decisions.”

SET PLAYS
Dead balls contributed nearly a quarter of all goals in the 2024/25
competition, with standout execution from Lyon and Real Madrid

SET PLAYS PAY DIVIDENDS
Set plays once again proved an effective source of goals in the
2024/25 UEFA Women’s Champions League. In total, 53 goals
(22%) were registered from corners, free-kicks and throw-ins,
with the total rising to 29% when the 14 penalties scored in the
competition were added.
Lyon proved most effective from set plays, Joe Montemurro’s side
registering 29% of their goals – eight in total – from dead balls in
their run to the semi-final. Other sides who profited from set plays
included Real Madrid, Bayern München and Barcelona. Madrid’s
seven set-play goals made up 32% of their total scored in the
competition, whilst Bayern’s six set-play strikes represented 33%
of their overall haul. Losing finalists Barcelona also scored six times
from set plays but this made up a lower proportion of their total
number of goals with 14%.
Some sides struggled to capitalise, four – Galatasaray, Celtic,
Hammarby and Juventus – failing to score a single goal from a
set play.

This disparity highlighted the importance of set-play
preparation, the benefits of expert set-piece takers and the value of
players who can make first contact from set plays delivered into the
penalty area.
A number of sides struggled to defend against set pieces,
Galatasaray conceding eight times – all of which were corners.
Others who failed to prevent goals from set plays included Twente,
who let in seven goals via that route, Roma and Celtic, who both
conceded five. Notably, finalists Barcelona conceded 50% of their
goals – four of the eight – from set plays. Norwegian club Vålerenga
were the only side not to concede a single goal from a set play.

THE VALUE OF CORNERS
Of the 638 corners taken in the 2024/25 Women’s Champions
League, 46 led to a goal being scored – an average of 14 corners
per goal. Lyon registered the most goals from corners with eight
(from 78 corners taken). However, it was Austrian side St. Pölten
who proved the most efficient, scoring twice from just six corners.
Real Madrid and Bayern München each scored six goals from 48
corners – averaging a goal every eight corners, which was above the
competition average. Finalists Barcelona scored four goals from 86
corners, equating almost 22 corners per goal.

GOALKEEPING
Although goalkeepers continued to be increasingly prominent
in building play, their primary objective remained preventing chances
and dealing with the threat from open play and set pieces
Goalkeepers in the semi-finals demonstrated a clear idea and intent
when building play from the back, explained Jim Stewart and Alex
Vencel of UEFA’s Goalkeeping Advisory Group.
“The goalkeepers of Barcelona, Arsenal, Chelsea and Lyon all
had a clear intent when building up play from restarts and open
play,” explained Stewart and Vencel. “The goalkeeper played a key
part in this phase of the game, displaying confidence and technical
expertise to find solutions and play a variety of passes – short,
medium and long – to maintain possession and initiate team plays.”
Many of the goalkeepers appearing in the quarter-finals adopted
a high support position to help recycle play across the back line. “The
assurance and composure of the goalkeeper to play high and be
the extra option to recycle play within team strategies was clearly
visible,” added UEFA’s Technical Observer Group.

“So, too, were the
technical abilities of goalkeepers and defenders to develop control
and composure as well as decision-making when dealing with
pressure close to their goal.”

BUILD-UP PLAY
Key roles for Van Domselaar, Coll and Hampton
During Arsenal’s 4-1 semi-final second-leg victory away to
Lyon, visiting goalkeeper Daphne van Domselaar displayed her
calmness in possession and ability to make line-breaking passes
during build-up play.
“Van Domselaar supports the team strategy, dealing with the pass
back and effectively maintaining team possession,” explained UEFA’s
goalkeeping group. “As Lyon start to press, she displays calmness in
maintaining her position to recycle play. As play develops, midfielder
Kim Little drops back to give an option to receive the pass from the
goalkeeper. Van Domselaar passes between the two Lyon strikers
and breaks the line, Little then has time and space to turn and link in
order to attack the Lyon goal.”
Barcelona’s Cata Coll and Chelsea’s Hannah Hampton
demonstrated similar composure and passing range during the semi-
final first leg between the two teams.

an accurate long ball from the ground to the striker.

UNDERSTANDING A GOALKEEPER’S

VARYING LEVEL OF INVOLVEMENT
When analysing goalkeeping performances in the
2024/25 UEFA Women’s Champions League, UEFA’s
technical experts assessed different types of involvement
and actions:
Regular involvement: Occurs where imminent
involvement with the ball is unlikely. The goalkeeper is in
observation and communication mode and takes up a
position relative to team shape
High involvement: Includes actively supporting and
preparing the execution of a particular team task
Ball involvement: When the goalkeeper is required to
be directly involved with the ball (e.g. handling, passing,
1v1 situation, putting pressure on the ball)

DEFENDING THE GOAL
A goalkeeper’s ability to make important saves had a major
impact on the match outcome from the quarter-finals onwards,
said UEFA’s goalkeeping experts. “The goalkeeper must have
high involvement through preparation in order to increase the
probability of making a save in demanding situations,” explained
Stewart and Vencel. “In general, at this level when teams of similar
strengths are competing and matches are in the balance, the
importance of the goalkeepers’ action to defending the goal has,
and will always be, the prime objective.
“To achieve this, the goalkeeper follows the same basic sequence:
observe events on the pitch; collect information and compare it
with previous experiences; select key aspects; decide how to act by
reacting to situational cues; execute the action appropriately.”
Both Arsenal’s Van Domselaar and Barcelona’s Coll
demonstrated excellent examples of defending the goal on the
way to the final. During Arsenal’s quarter-final second leg with
Real Madrid, Van Domselaar and the Arsenal defence recovered
and adjusted to defend against Real’s overload in the wide area.

When the Madrid player cut the ball back it deflected into the path
of the forward, who shot at goal. Van Domselaar quickly moved
across goal to make an excellent double save from the deflected
cutback cross.
“Barcelona’s Coll demonstrated the importance of positioning
and reacting to transitional phases during the final against
Arsenal.” After Coll received a pass back from a team-mate and
cleared the ball upfield, she immediately returned to a position
for the transitional phase. Arsenal’s Frida Maanum then gained
possession, drove towards goal and shot. Goalkeeper Coll showed
great agility and power to deflect the ball for a corner kick.”

Players stepped up at key points
“Big games come down to moments,” said Ange Postecoglou in
the aftermath of Tottenham Hotspur’s UEFA Europa League final
triumph. “We were really efficient with what we did.”
Spurs’ success in the all-English final against Manchester United
at San Mamés was built on Postecoglou’s players doing the right
thing at the key moments. There was a clear game plan, of which
more below, and with each player sticking rigorously to his task,
Spurs did enough to secure their first European trophy in 41 years –
and third triumph overall in this competition – by getting a goal late
in the first half through Brennan Johnson and then defending their
lead with strong organisation, determination and resilience.
Before elaborating on the details of their defensive plan, it is
worth considering the individual excellence displayed by players at
those key moments mentioned by Postecoglou.

Player of the Match
Cristian Romero led the Spurs defence superbly – and the top
screenshot on the right of him blocking off Rasmus Højlund in the
box is illustrative of his efforts.
“Romero dealt well with Manchester United’s direct play, he was
very aggressive with the defensive line and won the first contacts,”
said UEFA Technical Observer Steve Cooper of the Spurs captain’s
overall contribution. “In the second half, as Tottenham got deeper
and deeper, he showed real leadership. He constantly won duels and
his 1v1s. It was a well-rounded 90-minute performance in a game
where mistakes in that area of the pitch would have been costly.”
When United did have chances, individual moments of
brilliance kept Spurs’ lead intact. Witness the screenshot on
the bottom right of Micky van de Ven’s outstanding goal-line
clearance to deny Højlund in the 68th minute.

“This is a clear game plan that they’re absolutely committed to and

“Spurs press the ball in the mid-block when it goes wide and then
in the high block, they look to get pressure on the goalkeeper and

TRAINING

GROUND TIPS
Steve Cooper,
UEFA Technical Observer
Clearances
“There’s a craft and a technique to clearances and as with the Van
de Ven header [in ‘Spurs defending deep’ on page 12], this involves
body position and footwork. It’s not just heading either – can a
defender clear the ball with both feet? And when clearing the ball,
which areas do they want to clear it to and which areas do they not
want to clear it to?
“To work on this in training, you might have a 5v5 in the box with
each player assigned a defender to mark and balls coming in. You
could have three or four players dotted around the edge of the box
and every time a practice begins, they start with a cross and then,
when the ball comes out to them, they’ve got to put it back in. For
the defenders, you could give them target areas for their clearances
so it’s not just about getting the first contact and winning duels but
clearing the ball into the least dangerous position possible.”

Crosses and duels
“When defending crosses there are two coaching topics to follow
– first, you have the players who are looking to stop the cross and
their mindset must be, ‘Do whatever it takes to stop it’, be it by
winning the ball back or forcing the opponent back. For the players
in the box, meanwhile, their mindset has to be ‘This ball is coming in
so am I ready and how am I going to deal with it?’
“To begin with the players trying to stop the cross, they want to be
guiding the winger into a less dangerous situation and that might
be done by showing him onto a certain foot or into a certain area, or
it might mean slowing him down to allow for more cover to arrive.
“There is also the question of whether it’s a tackling situation or
a blocking situation. So what’s the best technical action to make?
Sometimes blocking can be less risky.

When you commit to a tackle,
you are committing your whole body so if you don’t win the ball, you
might find it hard to recover. There’s a technique to blocking so look
what a good body shape looks like when blocking. If you’re tackling,
meanwhile, which foot should it be and do you tackle with the inside
of your foot, the outside of your foot, or the toe?
“There are so many nuances and little technical details, such as
how close your defender’s feet should be when they’re jockeying
with the winger. Therefore the key thing is practice with different
scenarios in different-sized spaces. And the more decisions
players have to make, the better they become and the more
instinctively they react.
“For practice design, I’d suggest exposing players to 1v1s and
2v2s. Can they defend 1v1s in small areas? Can they defend 1v1s in
larger areas? And it’s important to set objectives.

For a defender in
a 1v1 or 2v2 situation, the objective could be to not let the player get   126
into the box or to win the ball before they get there, because it’s a
different situation once the ball is inside the box.
“You might also tell the players they’ve got to win the ball within
five seconds. Another approach would be bigger opposed practices
which could mean small-sided games with certain 1v1 or 2v2 zones
inside the pitch on it and the attacking players need to work the ball
out of those zones before they can cross or score a goal.”

LEAGUE PHASE
This was the first UEFA Europa League under the new format, with
a 36-team league phase replacing the previous 32-team group
stage. Excluding qualifying rounds, the total number of matches in
the competition increased from 141 to 189, with the final played at
the San Mamés Stadium in Bilbao.
Including the four rounds of qualification, 76 clubs from 41
of the 55 UEFA member nations participated and the 36 who
contested the league phase featured 13 former UEFA Cup/
Europa Legue finalists and six winners, among them Eintracht
Frankfurt and Manchester United, who had lifted the trophy
as recently as 2022 and 2017 respectively. The latter were the
highest-placed (11th) in the UEFA club rankings, heading 30
teams who appeared in the continent’s top 100. The lowest-
placed participants were Elfsborg of Sweden, ranked 302 and
who, along with Ferencváros of Hungary and Latvia’s RFS, edged
into the league phase via penalty shoot-outs in the play-off
round, while Olympiacos of Greece qualified as winners of the
2023/24 UEFA Conference League.

The league phase produced 401 goals at an average of 2.84
per game. Although Galatasaray finished 14th, they emerged
as the highest scorers among the 36 teams, with 19 strikes in
eight games, although they also conceded 16. Both Lazio and
Tottenham Hotspur registered 17, while Manchester United, sixth-
placed Lyon, eighth-placed Rangers, and 12th-placed Ajax all
scored 16 goals.
The 1.33 average goal difference in individual games was
the lowest across all UEFA’s men’s competitions, indicating how
competitive matches were in the Europa League. By comparison,
the average was 1.92 in the UEFA Champions League and
1.59 in the UEFA Conference League. Another symptom of
competitiveness was that the most common scoreline was 1-1.
This review of the league phase studies 11 matches and the
tactical themes that underpinned them.

Rayan Cherki
The Lyon forward showed all his
creativity in a breakthrough campaign
Rayan Cherki played in all 12 games as his Lyon side
reached the quarter finals. The 21-year-old scored four
goals and provided a competition-leading eight assists
as the Ligue 1 side scored 29 goals – a figure only
bettered by finalists Manchester United, who played
three games more.
All Cherki’s assists came in pairs: two in a 4-1 win at   his side a 3-2 lead with a left-foot strike at Old Trafford
Rangers on Matchday 2, two more in a 3-2 home win
against Eintracht Frankfurt on Matchday 6 and two
in both legs against FCSB in the round of 16 as Lyon
moved into the last eight with a 7-1 aggregate win over
the Romanian side.
Another graduate of Lyon’s celebrated academy
and an unused substitute as a 16-year-old when Rudi
Garcia’s side knocked Manchester City out of the
2019/20 Champions League quarter-finals, Cherki
has matured into a top player.

A two-footed creative
showman, in November 2024 he said: “Wherever I go,
I want to enjoy myself and entertain people because
when you see what happens pretty much everywhere in
matches, there’s not much entertainment on TV. I want
people to enjoy themselves when they’re watching TV.
And I hope to do so for the whole of my career.”
“Rayan has a lot of quality – all of football in Europe
knows him well,” said his club coach Paulo Fonseca in
April. “He worked a lot defensively and has improved
in this aspect for the team. After that, he must better
understand the space and the moments to do things.
He is a very strong player.”

“Rayan Cherki’s a talent, an exciting flair player who
has the ability to put that into productive performances,”
explained UEFA Technical Observer Steve Cooper. “His
technical ability, spatial awareness and decision-making
is very good. He dribbles well – but at the right time.
He can change and dictate the rhythm of the game.
It’s not just about moments – so that’s a talent. He can
play in a team structure but also off the cuff and with
instinctiveness to help the team and not just himself.”
“Rayan is someone a lot of clubs are watching,
an amazing talent who can decide a game in one
movement,” added his team-mate Nemanja Matić
ahead of the tie against Manchester United. Cherki lived
up to that praise in those matches, scoring a 95th-
minute equaliser in the first leg to make it 2-2 and giving
as Lyon came back from losing 2-0 to leading 4-2 with
ten men only to ultimately go down 5-4.

Cherki, who has 12 goals for France’s Under-21 side
and won a silver medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics
playing for a team coached by Thierry Henry, was
rewarded for his displays in the Europa League and
Ligue 1 with his first full senior call-up at the end of
the 2024/25 season. “Rayan could have been here
in March given what he has achieved with his club,"
said France coach Didier Deschamps. “He has been so
decisive in terms of his goals and his assists.”

GOALSCORING
Extra time supplied an unusually high number of
goals in 2024/25 and home advantage remained
significant, but scoring first was not as imperative
The 2024/25 Europa League season offered spectators
556 goals at an average of 2.94 per match. The
majority (58%) were scored by teams playing at home.
Seventy-six per cent of the goals (423) resulted from
open play, while the remaining 24% represented a fairly
standard return on set plays.
Goal timings
As usual, the second half was more prolific with 55%
of the goals scored after the break compared to 43%
during the opening period. Usually rather less, extra
time, so often a cagey half-hour, supplied the missing
2%. The five knockout round ties that required the
additional 30 minutes – two of them in the quarter-
finals – generated ten goals. Half of them were scored
between the 105th and 121st minutes of the 5-4
quarter-final epic between Manchester United and
Lyon, described by Steve Cooper, UEFA’s Technical
Observer at Old Trafford, as “an incredible finish to the
game.

Sometimes in football, everything goes out of
the window and you must create chaos.”
There had been a similar degree of anything goes
when Bodø/Glimt entertained Twente in the knockout
phase play-offs. After the second leg ended 4-4 on
aggregate after 90 minutes, the Norwegian side hit two
in the extra half-hour.
In normal time, the scoring rate increased towards
half-time; peaked in the first 15 minutes after the
break; and, unusually, dipped towards the end. Timings
of just under 10% of the total goals had a + sign in
them – almost three-quarters of those (71% to be
precise) during added time at the end of the second
half with teams often chasing an equaliser or a winner.
Statistics hint that half-time team talks also had an
effect. The most prolific segment was the period
between 45 and 60 minutes when 92 goals (17% of
the total) were scored.

Only eight of the season’s 189 matches remained
goalless: Viktoria Plzeň vs Ludogorets, Union Saint-
Gilloise vs Bodø/Glimt, Lazio vs Ludogorets, Olympiacos
vs Twente, Hoffenheim vs FCSB, Fenerbahçe vs Lyon,
FCSB vs Olympiacos (all in the league phase) and, in
the quarter-finals, Rangers vs Athletic Club. The last
two were affected by red cards.

Three of Fernandes’ goals
came in a 4-1 win against Real Sociedad in the last 16
second leg as he became the only player to score a
hat-trick in the competition last season. With four assists,
Fernandes was a key player and a contender for Player
of the Season; Young Player of the Season was Lyon’s
Rayan Cherki, who had 12 goals and assists in total.
Manchester United were comfortably the top scorers
across the competition with 35, though both Spurs and
Lazio registered a goal more in the league phase. United
were high scorers in the knockout stages, scoring four at
home to Real Sociedad, five at home to Lyon and three
away at Athletic Club in the semi-final first leg. Many of
these goals came in relatively short bursts – United led
3-0 at San Mamés at half-time in the semi-final opener.

United’s 5-4 extra time win against Lyon featured
more goals than any other game, or in the entire
history of the Europa League – another reason why
Fernandes and Cherki feature so prominently in the
goals and assists charts. Lyon were the second top
scorers in the whole competition, despite only reaching
the quarter-final stage. The other three teams in

Finishing off crosses
All but two of the 36 teams in the Europa League
scored open-play goals from crosses – the exceptions
Olympiacos and Qarabağ – but there were striking
differences in conversion rates. The most efficient team
was Ferencváros, who from a total of 90 deliveries
from wide areas, scored six of their 15 goals at the
competition’s best success ratio of 1:15. Numerically,
with the advantage of going all the way to the final,
Manchester United posted the highest goal total of
ten (from 176 crosses) which put them among a trio
separated by decimal points behind the Hungarian side.
The graphic below, featuring only the top 20 in terms of
conversion rates, shows that Ferencváros were twice as
effective as Galatasaray and semi-finalists Bodø/Glimt.
Conspicuous by their absence from the top 20 were
the other beaten semi-finalists, Athletic Club. The Basque
side delivered more crosses from the wide areas than
any other team in the competition, leading to 63 goal
attempts.

However, a finishing total of six goals left them
in 22nd place in the efficiency ratings with a ratio of one
success per 37 crosses. Similarly, Slavia Praha delivered
the most crosses per game, averaging 20, but three
goals signified a conversion ratio of 1:54. Anderlecht and
quarter-finalists Eintracht Frankfurt occupied the 33rd
and 34th places in the ranking with one goal apiece from
118 and 119 crosses respectively.

Pressing outcomes
Overall, ball-winning in the attacking third opened a
shorter route to goal, with teams averaging 4.9 shots
per game following a ball recovery in the attacking
third, either through a press to win the ball back or
transitional moments triggering second-wave attacks.
Stopping opposition passes
in their build-up
On average, teams attempted 144 passes from their
defensive third per game, with a success rate of 81%.
That meant that the opponents stopped 19% of
these forward passes. A team’s approach to pressing
in this area of the pitch had a great impact on this
figure. As shown in the chart, Slavia Praha who failed
to make it out of the league phase, led the way for
disrupting these passes, cutting out 29% of them. Nice
also enjoyed relative success, preventing 23% of the
opposition’s build-up passing – yet failed to win any of
their eight league phase fixtures.

Turning the spotlight on to teams who reached the
quarter-finals, we can see the variations in approach
with Manchester United stopping 22% of their
opponents’ passes from the defensive third compared
to the more conservative approaches of Rangers, Lyon,
Athletic Club and Lazio, who intercepted 19%. These
teams opted to try to recover the ball from a mid-block
when the opportunity for high pressing had gone.
Tactical variations in
the knockout phase
As shown at the bottom right, the first leg between
Fenerbahçe and Rangers provided a good example
of a team conceding possession higher up the pitch
and preferring to drop into a compact mid-block, with
wing-backs pressing press in the wide areas. The tactic
worked well for the Glasgow club in Istanbul, where they
recorded a 3-1 win. “We were very bad everywhere,” said
Fenerbahçe coach Jose Mourinho. “I don’t think it’s fair to
say that we were bad defensively because we were very
bad everywhere.”
“I thought it was a really good performance,” said
Rangers coach Barry Ferguson.

“The players took in
every single thing that me and my coaching staff went
over on the training ground. Overall, it’s a brilliant result
but there’s no way that I’m getting carried away. This is
only half-time in the tie.”
Ferguson’s cautious approach was vindicated by a
0-2 defeat in the second leg at Ibrox, sending the tie to
penalties where Rangers prevailed 3-2. After his side had
edged through, Ferguson said: “When you play against
really good teams, they’re going to hurt you in stages
and you have to let them have the ball. I’m proud of the
players and I’m just delighted for the club as whole.”

TRAINING

GROUND TIPS
Steve Cooper,
UEFA Technical Observer
Preparing a defensive plan
Off the pitch, you can show how you’re going to defend in certain
areas – showing clips and using the tactics board. On the training
pitch you might walk through scenarios but also try to create game-
like situations, such as putting the opposition shape against your
shape and recreating possible passing tactical moves that can be
deployed by the opposition.
When you coach these real-life scenarios, there are always ‘what-
ifs’ arising. What if the full-back doesn’t get pressure on the ball? The
wingers aren’t in a position to defend the inside? That’s when you’re
able to talk about the trade-off between what you’re willing to give up
and what you’re hoping to do.
When it comes to practice design, you might zone off the pitch with
certain players only going in areas to mimic the opposition’s shape
and passing sequences. If you’re working on the high press, you might
use half the pitch, with the opposition trying to get over the halfway
line.

Or have a coned line in the middle of your defensive half and set
the opposition the challenge of getting over this line.
There’s no exact age to start working on his level of detail, but
by the time a young player reaches 15 or 16 and begins to really
understand the game and how to be part of a tactical plan, that’s
when you might start drip-feeding relevant information.
When defending crosses there are two coaching topics to follow –
first, you have the players who are looking to stop the cross and their

Gundersen
