deal with
a cross
mindset must be, ‘Do whatever it takes to stop it’, be it by winning the
ball back or forcing opponents back. Secondly, for the players in the
box, their mindset has to be, ‘This ball is coming in, so am I ready and
how am I going to deal with it?’
With the players trying to stop the cross, they want to be guiding
the winger into a less dangerous situation and that might be done
by showing him on to a certain foot or into a certain area, or it might
mean slowing him down to allow for more cover to arrive.
There’s also the question of whether it’s a tackling situation or
a blocking situation. So what’s the best technical action to make?
Sometimes blocking can be less risky. When you commit to a tackle,
you are committing your whole body, so if you don’t win the ball, you
might find it hard to recover.

There’s a technique to blocking, so look what a good body shape
looks like when blocking. If you’re tackling, meanwhile, which foot
should it be, and do you tackle with the inside of your foot, the
outside of your foot, or the toe?
There are many nuances and little technical details, such as how
close your defender’s feet should be when they’re jockeying with the
winger. Therefore, the key thing is practice with different scenarios in
different-sized spaces. And the more decisions players must make,
the better they become and the more instinctively they react.
For practice design, I’d suggest exposing players to 1v1s and 2v2s.
Can they defend 1v1s in small areas or 1v1s in larger areas? It’s
important to set objectives. For a defender in a 1v1 or 2v2 situation,
the objective could be to not let the player get into the box or to win
the ball before they get there, because it’s a different situation once
the ball is inside the box.

You might also tell the players they’ve got to win the ball within
five seconds. Another approach would be bigger opposed practices
– small-sided games with 1v1 or 2v2 zones inside the pitch. The
attacking players need to work the ball out of those zones before
they can cross or score a goal.

Free-kicks
There were only five successes from direct free-kicks
over the course of the season’s 189 games. Goals from
indirect free-kicks were less of a rarity, Manchester
United and Ajax notching three apiece to lead the
field. But Eintracht Frankfurt’s second goal in the 3-1
away win against Beşiktaş stood out as a creative,
well-rehearsed set play. A free-kick was played to
Omar Marmoush, whose curling right-footed diagonal
was nodded by Robin Koch into the middle of the box
where the unmarked Dina Ebimbe side-footed past the
goalkeeper.
“A set-piece routine like this demands flawless timing
and technical excellence,” said Jan Peder Jalland,
UEFA Technical Observer. “Frankfurt strategically
split their front five during the free-kick from the
centre, positioning players to exploit both left and
right channels. In this instance, they chose the
shorter route – a quick pass from slightly right to the
left, followed by an inswinging cross. This approach
created advantageous angles while posing significant
challenges for the Beşiktaş defence.”

Build-up
Onana positioned himself deeper for back passes,
allowing more time to deliver the next pass. This
tended to slow the game down and oblige team-
mates to build from a deeper area of the pitch
– in contrast to his modus operandi at previous
clubs. When pressed, Onana took no risks and
played long towards the main striker (with limited
success). Most of his goal-kicks were also hit long.
Onana frequently played long balls under pressure:
54 throughout the competition with a success rate
of 44%. When pressed by opponents, 38 were either
short or medium passes. No less than 71% of his goal
kicks were long, compared with 19% short-distance
deliveries and 10% medium-length passes.
Vicario of Spurs took few risks when playing out,
notably in the final. This appeared to be a clear team
tactic as he regularly played long into a wide area when
given time.

On the occasions when Vicario was pressed
quickly after a back pass, the Italian played high and
long with very little thought of playing into an area
where his team could retain possession. Goal kicks were
also played long and high to one side of the pitch away
from the opposition centre-backs – another team tactic
which allowed team-mates to gather on one side of the
pitch and focus on winning the second ball. During the
earlier knockout games when playing at home, he was
prepared to take greater risks during build-up, playing
a wider variety of long and short passes with healthy
success rates.

collectively covered more ground than any of the other

the top ten of the overall ranking.
From a coaching perspective, distance-covered
statistics are a perennial topic for discussion, with one
side of the debate arguing that the most impressive
data often corresponds to teams obliged to spend more
time out of possession and therefore cover greater
distances while chasing the ball. The final was a case
in point. Manchester United dominated possession by
65% to 35%; Spurs covered 112,116 metres to United’s
104,922 – a difference of 7%.
The collective rankings for the season provide further
evidence.

Of the teams who reached the quarter-finals,
only Bodø/Glimt and Spurs appear in the top ten in the
distance-covered averages while the other two semi-
finalists, Athletic Club and Manchester United, are right at
the foot of the table. Five of the top ten were eliminated
in the league phase. But the statistics clearly show that
Bodø/Glimt’s average distance was 4.4% higher than
anybody else’s and a full 12% greater than the duo at the
foot of the table. Extra time, incidentally, has been excluded.
Similar parameters prevail in the top ten of the
individual ranking where, apart from the Norwegian
club’s trio, none played for teams who progressed
beyond the Round of 16 and five of the other seven

THE COACHES
The UEFA Coaching Convention sets minimum
standards for national associations and offers
them guidance, information and support
The UEFA Coaching Convention provides a benchmark
for the education of coaches within Europe, helping to
raise the quality of coaching across the continent and
facilitating the free movement of qualified professionals
around UEFA’s member associations. The value of Article
8 of the convention is worth highlighting as it promotes
reality-based learning – a key tool for coaches today.
Informal learning
UEFA supports informal learning – learning that is incidental
or self-directed and not led by another person. Examples
include everyday experiences, observing or talking to other
coaches and self-study. The more insights coaches gain,
the better they can discover what works for them in practice.
Understanding how to apply knowledge in coaching is a key
part of development.

Reality-based learning
Reality-based learning is beneficial because by
ensuring the learning environment is realistic, coaches
can prepare themselves and their players for the
real-life situations they may face. As UEFA technical
instructor Phil Church said: “If you don’t do reality-based

Preparing for game-realistic
scenarios
These can be structured moments such as patterns of
play and help coaches build a game model and develop
player understanding of key principles. Structured practice
provides more control to create the pictures they want to
see but should not restrict decision-making. Opposition
analysis can offer insight, but coaches must adapt to
challenges on matchday. This may involve tactical changes
or substitutions. In the UEFA Conference League final,
Chelsea coach Enzo Maresca introduced Jadon Sancho,
a winger who dribbles and drives forward. As Church
said: “He makes the defence drop, which is a different
tactical problem.”
Coaches should create environments where players
identify problems and find solutions. Kris Van Der Haegen,
coach education director at the Belgian FA, said: “You need
to give them the space to try out what they have. If they
recognise the structure of the opposition and they know
their role, they can express themselves in a creative way.”
Unstructured moments such as transition are harder to
prepare for.

However, by developing clear principles of play
and regularly exposing players to realistic scenarios, they
can respond more effectively.

Despite Betis’ early control, Maresca did not overhaul the system

A combination of personnel changes – starting with Reece James

the ball, I’m just going to go [forward]’ – and it worked.”
The Chelsea No10 replaced Isco as the outstanding player on the
pitch by setting up two goals in six minutes. “Palmer delivered two

LEAGUE PHASE
The 2024/25 UEFA Conference League began with a new 36-team
league phase, marking a significant shift from the previous group
stage structure as clubs competed in a single league table. Each team
played six fixtures – three at home and three away – resulting in an
increase from 96 to 108 matches.
The top eight teams in the league phase advanced directly to
the round of 16, while those ranked from ninth to 24th entered the
knockout phase play-offs, with the ninth to 16th-placed teams given
home advantage for the second leg. The teams placed 25th to 36th
ended their campaigns at the conclusion of the league phase.
Former UEFA Champions League winners Chelsea proved their
credentials by registering six wins out of six to take top spot. The
English side, the highest-ranked team in the UEFA coefficient,
conceded only five times and racked up 26 goals, including an 8-0 rout
of the club with the lowest UEFA coefficient ranking, Armenian Premier
League runners-up Noah.

The league phase produced 320 goals, 77% from open play and
23% from set pieces – a trend observed closely by UEFA’s Technical
Observer Group. The UEFA Technical Observers explore various themes
in possession, including ingenuity to find the spare man in build-up play,
the battle for pockets of space in midfield and fluid combination play in
the attacking third while filling the box with attackers to seize on crossing
opportunities after clever switches of play.
Out of possession, the effectiveness of coordinated high pressing
and the importance of game nous to disrupt an opponent’s build-
up play caught the attention. The UEFA Technical Observers also
noted the effectiveness of cohesion and compactness among
the stronger teams when defending in the mid and low block, with
a particular emphasis on protecting the centre of the pitch and
defending the box.

HEIDENHEIM v CHELSEA
Mid-block causes Chelsea concern
On Matchday 4 Heidenheim posed problems for Chelsea with
a disciplined and compact mid-block that kept the result in the
balance until an 86th-minute Mykhailo Mudryk strike sealed a 2-0
victory. The Premier League side owed a debt of gratitude to their
goalkeeper Filip Jørgensen for several smart stops, including a
double save in the second half to preserve the one-goal lead.
When Heidenheim chose the moment to initiate a high press from
the mid-block – often seizing on a backwards pass in the defensive
third as a trigger – Chelsea responded with guile, intelligence and
bravery to overcome the 1v1 pressure approach from the home
side. But how did they manage it?
As well as impressing with his shot-stopping, Jørgensen held the
key in possession with the ball at his feet when confronted by the
initial press. Jørgensen tended to invite the first pressure before
finding the spare man behind the pressing attacker or via a bounce
pass from a retreating midfielder.

The speed and timing of the
movements by the Chelsea players to escape markers and create
angles to receive, offered clear options to progress the play. In many
cases of successful build-up play in the defensive third, one and two-

applied significant pressure and pushed Djurgården deep

Real Betis’ trip to the KAA Gent Arena to face the Belgian side in

a tight affair. Separated by just one place in the UEFA coefficient
ranking – Gent in 48th, just ahead of their visitors – and just two

both teams had reason to believe they could progress beyond the
stage at which they were eliminated last season.
That was exactly the way the match began, with both sides intent
on attack.

UEFA Technical Observer Leif Gunnar Smerud noted the
home team’s early strategy of targeting the big spaces behind the
Betis defence, especially in wide areas. “It was quite direct and
physical,” he said.
“It’s perhaps the Belgian way,” he explained. “Fast and direct,
often with long passes to the strikers and with midfielders surging
forward to win the second ball and outrun their opponents.” Smerud
highlighted the impact of striker Dante Vanzeir, midfielder Atsuki
Ito and wing-back Matisse Samoise in the raids targeting the
opposition’s left side.
After a goalless first half, however, the game changed just two
minutes into the second period, when the Conference League
debutant Antony opened the scoring for Betis with a low, curling shot
into the bottom corner of the net from the edge of the penalty area.

Chelsea laid the foundations for a 3-1 aggregate victory against
Copenhagen with a first-leg win in Denmark in which they were forced
to adapt their initial approach to finally gain the upper hand in midfield.
Real Betis, meanwhile, had to be patient to get the better of Vitória SC,
eventually prevailing 6-2 over the two legs thanks to a well-organised
attacking approach expertly spearheaded by Cédric Bakambu.
COPENHAGEN v CHELSEA
The battle for midfield supremacy
“Every team is trying to find central overloads with their most
creative players between the lines,” said UEFA Technical Observer
David Adams. This reflection came after watching Chelsea earn a
2-1 advantage away at Copenhagen in a first-leg encounter marked
by a battle for supremacy in the middle in which two rival attacking
trends were evident.
“In possession, Chelsea used three plus two in the create phase,”
explained Adams, who noted the patterns in a 3-2-2-3 set-up seeking
to feed the two No10s – Cole Palmer and Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall –
between the lines.

“Copenhagen matched them up with three forwards
and two midfielders to prevent central line breaks,” said Adams.
The compact mid-block shape forced Palmer and Dewsbury-Hall
to seek space outside the two defensive midfielders, where the
outside centre-backs and wing-backs were ready “to be aggressive
by jumping to apply pressure”.
Copenhagen’s strategy denied the leading goalscorers in the
league phase a shot on target in a goalless first half.
The second trend involved the home side’s attacking approach.
Chelsea went 4-4-2 out of possession, with the high left-winger
retreating to full-back when the ball was lost. “Copenhagen’s in-
possession shape, 3-4-3, seemed intent on exploiting this system,”
said Adams, noting how the positions of the home side’s diamond
midfield four opened spaces to exploit.
At times they penetrated with passes or forward runs with the ball
from centre-backs, exposing the lack of cover in front of Chelsea’s
back line, especially when Enzo Maresca switched to one holding
midfielder in a bolder 4-1-4-1 after the break.

High press pays off
However, Copenhagen’s only goal – a late header by Gabriel
Pereira – came after Chelsea had established a two-goal lead.
“The second goal [by Enzo Fernández] was crucial,” said Adams.
“It came from a brilliant dead-ball high press by Chelsea. Really
aggressive, forcing a turnover in a man-to-man press with left-
back [Marc] Cucurella advancing high.”
Maresca’s bold substitutions at half-time and switch to 4-1-4-1
in possession helped Chelsea gain “more control of the middle
against the diamond” according to Adams. “It helped swing the
momentum of the match.”
Adams hailed the “timing and bravery of Chelsea’s full-backs to go
high and leave team-mates 1v1 in the back line” as a lesson in modern
defending. “Young centre-backs need to be developed to have the
athleticism and ability to defend in central and wide areas,” he said.

Isco
The 33-year-old was the crucial figure in Betis'
march to the final, with and without the ball
“Isco was 45 minutes away from leading his club to historic glory in
Europe,” said Haakon Lunov, UEFA Technical Observer. “He was the
outstanding player in the first half of the final.”
Although Chelsea – and Cole Palmer, in particular – intervened to
kill off Real Betis’ dreams, Isco left a lasting impression in Wroclaw.
At half-time the Spaniard ranked first for key passes (three), balls
in behind (seven) and line-breaking passes (nine). But he also
led without the ball too, registering the joint-highest number of
pressures (17) as Betis successfully disrupted Chelsea’s build-up
and led to the opening goal, which offered a glimpse of the potency
of the 33-year-old creative heartbeat of Los Verdiblancos.
“Isco’s assist was incredible,” said Jan Peder Jalland, UEFA
Technical Observer. “The reverse pass to find Abdessamad
Ezzalzouli shows a high level of ability. It’s all excellent.

The first
touch, the quick scan and then finding the player [Ezzalzouli], who is
actually behind him.”
Isco’s “incredible” moment was his third assist in nine
appearances and 632 minutes during the UEFA Conference
League campaign in which he formed a potent attacking unit
alongside the competition’s second-highest goalscorer, Cédric
Bakambu, and wingers Antony and Ezzalzouli.

across 153 matches — an average of 2.95 per game, or

inaugural league phase of the tournament. Nearly eight
months later, Moises Caicedo sealed the title for Chelsea
in added time with the 451st and final goal of the campaign.
Over three-quarters (350) came from open play and
over half (57%) were scored by the home team. There
were 12 own goals and 28 from penalties – with five spot
kicks converted in the Matchday 5 fixtures alone. Only
five matches ended goalless, four of which came in the
league phase.

Noah. A month later Fiorentina hit seven without reply at

Team productivity
Chelsea topped the charts for goals, scoring 42 times – 12
more than semi-finalists Fiorentina. Runners-up Real Betis
(23) and losing semi-finalists Djurgården (19) made up the top
six along with Celje (25) and Jagiellonia (20), all comfortably
above the average for the tournament, which was 11.
In terms of expected goals, Chelsea were ahead
of the pack again with 28.4. But they also outperformed their
xG by the biggest margin of any other team, ending up with
a positive margin of 13.6. Cercle Brugge came next with an
overperformance of 5.0 on an xG of 11.0.
Leading the way
Enzo Maresca’s side continued their productive exploits all
the way to the final after registering the highest figure in
the league phase, when Marc Guiu recorded a personal xG
overperformance of 3.1 with six goals. The teenage attacker
finished the tournament as third-highest scorer despite
playing no part in the knockout phase until the closing
minutes of the final due to injury.

Jagiellonia’s predatory striker Afimico Pululu took the
plaudits as leading scorer with eight goals, five in the league
phase and three in the knockouts. “Pululu was strong,
always in the box, seeking out the first contact and a very
good finisher,” said Dimitris Papadopoulos, UEFA Technical
Observer. Pululu’s eighth and final goal – a stunning
overhead kick against Cercle Brugge in the last 16 – was
awarded second place in the Goal of the Season ranking.
There were only two hat-tricks in the tournament – Guiu
against Shamrock Rovers on Matchday 6 and Kevin Denkey
for Cercle Brugge against St. Gallen on Matchday 1.
Two teenagers made Conference League history. First,
17-year-old James Wilson claimed the mantle
of youngest-ever scorer in the competition with a strike
for Heart of Midlothian against Petrocub on Matchday 6.
A couple of months later, Shamrock Rovers striker Michael
Noonan eclipsed this record by sealing victory at Molde in
the first leg of the knockout phase play-off aged just
16 years 197 days.

In a trend that mirrored the UEFA Europa League, the
opening 30 minutes of the second half proved bountiful for

IN POSSESSION
There were contrasting approaches to building from the back while
further forward the wings offered a key route into the final third,
though narrow inside zones paid off for Chelsea and Celje
bUILDINg THE PLAy
Building from goal kicks is no longer just a restart – it has
become a key strategic phase in modern football. Across the
2024/25 UEFA Conference League, teams demonstrated
tactical variation in how they initiated possession, whether
playing short to bait pressure or launching directly to bypass it.
One of the major coaching debates centres on the identity
of the kick taker. A significant majority of the 2,000-plus
restarts in the competition (85%) were taken by the
goalkeeper – equating to around 14 per game. An alternative
approach, using an outfield player to take the restart, was
typically reserved for situations involving aggressive player-
to-player pressing from high opponents. In these cases, the
goalkeeper remained central while the defender initiated play.

Since pressing teams often locked on to outfield players in a
man-to-man scheme, the unmarked goalkeeper was free to
receive and dictate the next phase.
Distance and difference
As the graphic on the far right illustrates, Chelsea registered
the shortest average distance for first passes from goal
kicks (16.5m). This was nearly half the tournament average
(32.7m) and less than one-third of Cercle Brugge’s average
(57.6m). The huge range – and relatively long average
distances – suggest that the use of very short passes from
goal kicks to bait the opposition into a high press and find a
spare man can increase further at the elite level.
The second graphic shows the variety of approaches
concerning the taker too. TSC Bačka Topola (40%), SK Rapid
and Chelsea (both 35%) were the most frequent users of
the outfield starter strategy, whereas the average was just
15% and four teams chose to use only their goalkeeper. The
selection of the starting player reflects a strategic choice
reflected in the stark difference in average length of passes.

From a goalkeeper, the average distance was 37 metres –
nearly four times as long as the outfield figure (9.6m).

Possession vs progression
While the choice of kick-taker and pass length influenced
structure, equally important was how teams turned build-up into
territorial progression. Panathinaikos progressed to the final third
on 32% of their goal kicks – the highest rate in the competition.
SK Rapid registered the second-highest success rate (28%) and
the highest total number of entries (20) from more attempts. The
top ten also included the finalists, Real Betis and Chelsea. The
Seville-based side took 92 goal kicks, second only to Djurgården
(95). However, Manuel Pellegrini’s charges managed to reach
the final third only 15% of the time, just below the tournament
average of 17%.
Chelsea’s high possession (63%) and measured build-up under
Enzo Maresca showed their preference for slow tempo control.
This patience meant fewer direct passes from the back and
a greater emphasis on short combinations to manipulate the
press.

Only 26% of Chelsea’s open-play passes went from the
defensive third to the middle or final thirds; every other team had
at least 31%. That telling statistic showed Enzo Maresca’s version
of penetration involved more patience than any other team and
decision-making devolved to players on whether to retain or
progress as the game developed.

CHANCE CREATION
Creative play in the 2024/25 UEFA Conference League came
in many forms — from wide channel dominance to incisive
line-breaking passes. With all teams willing to sit in a low block
at times, the progressive pursuit of space and overloads led
to the wide channels more often than not. As the first graphic
reveals, the wings were the destination for 56% of all passes
into the final third. The central zone proved marginally more
attractive than the half-spaces as an alternative.
Chelsea’s figures mirrored the overall statistics closely,
with 14% apiece in the half-spaces and 27% going to each
wing. The eventual champions’ high possession and creative
dynamism in the pockets perhaps explain why they managed
18% of passes into the tightly-patrolled central channel, three
percentage points above the overall tournament figure. In total,
22 different Chelsea players managed to find a team-mate
in the central channel, with Tosin Adarabioyo (16 times) and
Cesare Casadei (12) leading the way. The screenshot on the
right shows Adarabioyo finding Enzo Fernández in the inside-
right channel.

Not all sides were so versatile in their approach. For example,
Shamrock Rovers targeted the right channel with 42% of balls,
often utilising the forward passing strengths of defender Daniel
Cleary. In contrast, only 20% of the Irish team’s passes went to
the left channel.

Switching play
While wide channel entries were the most frequent, top teams
also relied on switching play and manipulating compact blocks
through movement between the lines. Fiorentina’s ability to switch
the point of attack was hailed by the UEFA Technical Observers as
a potent asset. As the graphic on the bottom left shows, the Viola
managed the most diagonal switches of play (39) – defined as a
pass of at least 30 metres to a wide channel from the opposite wing
or half-space. Robin Gosens, the attacking left wing-back named
in the Team of the Season, was often a target as Fiorentina sought
to exploit the weak defensive side after a switch from the right.
Jonathan Ikoné, Dodô and Fabiano Parisi gained success at times
on the opposite side. In total, their switches led to six shots.
Runners-up Real Betis managed one more shot at goal from
fewer switches (34). Frank Schmidt’s Heidenheim were even more
productive.

With Jonas Föhrenbach prominent on the left and
Omar Haktab Traoré on the right, the Bundesliga side equalled
Fiorentina’s shot tally from one-third fewer switches.
Receiving between the lines in the final
“The ability to move cleverly and receive the ball in a position to
face forward in the final third are key strengths,” said the UEFA
Technical Observer David Adams after the final. Two of the creators
named in the Team of the Season’s midfield three alongside Celje’s
Svit Sešlar excelled in this domain. Player of the Season Isco
dominated the first half for Real Betis “in prime position to pose
maximum threat”, according to Adams. Chelsea’s Enzo Fernández
proved instrumental in the second-half comeback. Both players
received between the lines nine times in the match. While Cole
Palmer was rightly hailed for his “moments of magic” with two assists
after the break, Fernández also excelled by receiving between the
lines in the build-up to two goals. Chelsea’s dominance of possession
is reflected in the fact that they had four of the top six spots.

Finding the gap: the final showdown
Fernández was edged out by Real Betis’ Pablo Fornals as the chief
architect of line-breaking passes in the final. David Adams hailed the
closely related skillsets – “game awareness and vision to find solutions
to eliminate pressure” – required to both thrive on the half-turn in the
pocket and to pick out the forward pass. Although Fornals was joined
by Isco in the top five line-breakers, three of Chelsea’s chief recipients
of passes in advanced areas also stood out with forward passing.
Palmer’s line-breaking tally was five short of Fernández and
Moises Caicedo. Not all line-breaking passes are equal, of course.
Caicedo bypassed 53 players with his 15 passes, a tally exceeded
only by two of Chelsea’s central defenders, Benoît Badiashile and
Trevoh Chalobah. In terms of the number of defenders taken out,
the Ecuador international bypassed eight, just one behind
the second-half creator-in-chief Palmer.

POSSESSION
Chelsea were the most effective in turning high regains into chances
and goals, the mid-block organisation of Real Betis and Djurgården
impressed and Celje deployed a low block to good effect
HIgH PRESS
Stealing the ball high to exploit momentary instability
in opponents is a big draw for teams in a high block.
But topping the charts for the number of successful
turnovers in these moments does not automatically
translate to more goals and victories. By way of illustration,
neither of the teams with the joint-highest average number
of turnovers in the final third progressed beyond the
quarter-finals. SK Rapid were denied a place in the semi-
finals by Djurgården while Cercle Brugge bowed out in
the last 16 at the hands of Jagiellonia.
Seizing the moment
In contrast, the eventual champions Chelsea stole the
ball less often in high-pressing actions – 14.8 times,
slightly above the competition average of 13.2. However,
they stood out in two key metrics that offered a clearer
indicator of high-pressing effectiveness.

Firstly, the Premier League side led the way with the
highest proportion of their total regains (36%) in the
highest part of the pitch.
More pertinently, they seized the moment with
conviction, scoring 16 goals from these situations –
amounting to one for every 12 regains.
Chelsea’s ability to lock the opposition in their defensive
third by committing players high to regain possession
or be ready to win second balls was noted by David
Adams, UEFA Technical Observer, after their 2-1 win at
Copenhagen in the round of 16 first leg.

ATTACk TO DEfENCE
Developing the mindset to come alive in transitions offers
multiple rewards in the modern game, where well-structured
and robust defences can often effectively resist organised and
controlled attacks.
Some teams deployed bold counter-pressing strategies
to allow them to dial up the intensity by sustaining an attack
against a deep-lying defensive block. This aggressive approach
offers the twin benefit of disrupting the opponents’ strategy of
sitting in a deep block ready to spring counterattacks.
Counter-pressing kings
The team with the third-highest average for ball possession
– TSC Bačka Topola (57%) – led the pack on the number
of counter-pressing actions per 90 minutes too (45.6%),
which suggests they had some success in transitions to
sustain attacks.
As the chart shows, the Serbian side’s players managed a
counter-pressing action on average once every two minutes.
In terms of efficiency, they regained the ball in 13% of these
actions.

Noah, who exited at the league phase after finishing
31st, boasted the highest figure on this score, 16%.
TSC’s dual approach of controlled attacks and fierce
counter-pressing helped propel them out of the league
phase – one of six teams in the top ten on the chart to
advance to the knockout phase play-offs or beyond.
The screenshot offers a glimpse of their aggressive
approach on Matchday 2 against Legia Warszawa. The
left-sided centre-back Vukašin Krstić reacts to the loss of
possession by jumping to pressure the Legia winger and

transition offers an opportunity to exploit the brief opening
in Legia’s structure as they switch to offensive mode.

Building the foundation
The evolution of the goalkeeper’s role in the modern
elite game was evident throughout. All phases of the
game came under the spotlight, starting with one of
the biggest areas of development for the goalkeeping
skillset: the ball at the feet in build-up.
The quarter-finals onwards offered a true showcase
of versatility on the ball. “The goalkeepers showed
great variety with possession-based build-up but
also more direct play,” noted Jan Erik Stinessen and
Tomislav Butina of the UEFA Goalkeeper Expert Group.
“They were comfortable on the ball and assessed the
situations and climate of the match well.”
Winners Chelsea proved an interesting case study.

Usually in 1-4-3-3 from goal kicks, Enzo Maresca’s
side constantly involved the goalkeeper, offering him
three clear options in possession: playing through the
high press, going long to the striker or passing into
a midfielder to switch play. Once they advanced out
of the penalty area, Filip Jørgensen would step up to
form a back four as they switched to a 1-3-2-5 setup.
“Jørgensen dictated the tempo,” noted Stinessen and
Butina. “He was comfortable staying on the ball, waiting
to attract pressure before finding the free player.”
The examples opposite illustrate his composure in
two matches. Receiving a back pass wide of his goal
against Djurgården, Jørgensen performs a neat one-
touch turn to escape pressure and release.
The second example shows calmness under more
concerted pressure against Legia Warszawa in the
quarter-final second leg. Again, Jørgensen helps
his side retain possession to find a way out. “His
actions were executed with high risk, but he remained
composed,” noted the UEFA Goalkeeper Expert Group.

In this particular match, he racked up 42 short
and medium passes – one of the highest goalkeeper
tallies of any match in the tournament – and four long
passes. Given that 19 of these were executed under
direct pressure, the successful completion rate of
45 out of 46 highlights just how crucial Jørgensen’s
composure was to the Chelsea gameplan.

The importance of a goalkeeper’s “synchronisation”
with defenders while showing perception, flexibility
and fine technique are emphasised by the analysis

count. The map shows the concentration of the

The “high involvement” goalkeeper comes into their
own in this close-quarters battle near the goal. The
UEFA Goalkeeper Expert Group picked out Fiorentina’s

exponents of the art of defending the goal.

THE COACHES
The UEFA Coaching Convention sets minimum
standards for national associations and offers
them guidance, information and support
The UEFA Coaching Convention provides a benchmark
for the education of coaches within Europe, helping to
raise the quality of coaching across the continent and
facilitating the free movement of qualified professionals
around UEFA’s member associations. The value of Article
8 of the convention is worth highlighting as it promotes
reality-based learning – a key tool for coaches today.
Informal learning
UEFA supports informal learning – learning that is incidental
or self-directed and not led by another person. Examples
include everyday experiences, observing or talking to other
coaches and self-study. The more insights coaches gain,
the better they can discover what works for them in practice.
Understanding how to apply knowledge in coaching is a key
part of development.

Preparing for game-realistic
scenarios
These can be structured moments such as patterns of
play and help coaches build a game model and develop
player understanding of key principles. Structured practice
provides more control to create the pictures they want to
see but should not restrict decision-making. Opposition
analysis can offer insight, but coaches must adapt to
challenges on matchday. This may involve tactical changes
or substitutions. In the UEFA Conference League final,
Chelsea coach Enzo Maresca introduced Jadon Sancho,
a winger who dribbles and drives forward. As Church
said: “He makes the defence drop, which is a different
tactical problem.”
Coaches should create environments where players
identify problems and find solutions. Kris Van Der Haegen,
coach education director at the Belgian FA, said: “You need
to give them the space to try out what they have. If they
recognise the structure of the opposition and they know
their role, they can express themselves in a creative way.”
Unstructured moments such as transition are harder to
prepare for.

However, by developing clear principles of play
and regularly exposing players to realistic scenarios, they
can respond more effectively.

moments in the second phase from set pieces. It is
important for coaches to have a strategy to ensure security
behind the ball as their players will be faced with either

required to defend a potential counterattack.

INTRODUCTION

INTRODUCTION
UEFA’s Technical Observer Group were on hand to
analyse all the action as the tournament continued
to reach new heights on and off the pitch
This review of UEFA Women’s EURO 2025 provides a record of a
tournament which comprised 31 matches across 26 days between
2 and 27 July 2025.
Held in eight venues across Switzerland, this was the third 16-
team Women’s EURO final tournament and it had the tagline ‘The
summit of emotions’ – which proved fitting given the way it took
the women’s game in Europe to fresh heights.
With an overall attendance of 657,291 and 29 of the 31 fixtures
sold out, the finals set a record for spectators at a Women’s EURO
while on the pitch there were an unprecedented number of goals
scored – a total of 106 at a rate of 3.42 per game.
And it ended with Sarina Wiegman’s England becoming the
second team after Germany to win back-to-back Women’s
EUROs thanks to their final triumph over world champions Spain.

The improved technical quality on display was matched by the
impressive game understanding and fitness exhibited by players
who met the demands, both in terms of in-game tactical changes
and physical endurance, of a knockout stage rich in drama and
intensity as five of the seven matches required extra time and
three went all the way to penalties.
Surveying the action at every match were members of UEFA’s
Technical Observer Group. From the stands, the observers
assessed the proceedings from a coaching perspective, identifying
key tactical themes for further analysis – such as the use of
combination play to unlock defences and strategies for exploiting
space behind opposition back lines.

BELGIUM 0-1 ITALY (MD1)

WHEN 5-3-2 MEETS 5-3-2
The opening fixture for these Group B rivals was a
low-risk affair in which both sides set up with a 1-5-3-2
and looked for defensive control, trying to maintain an
extra player against the opposition forwards.
In the first half, as illustrated by the first image on
the right, Italy looked to draw out the Belgium wing-
back on one side and take advantage of the half-spaces
behind – through a run by a midfield player or striker.
Alternately, they looked to exploit space on the other
side with the opposite wing-back.
In response, Belgium adjusted their defensive
organisation in the second half, keeping both wing-
backs behind the ball while a centre-back stepped
forward to press instead. This change reduced Italy’s
ability to exploit the half-spaces compared with earlier
in the match.
Another detail, noted by the UEFA Technical
Observer Group, was how Belgium looked to disrupt
the Italy shape.

As the second image on the right
shows, Belgium built with a single central attacker,
Tessa Wullaert, while their other forward, Hannah
Eurlings, drifted to the left wing to receive diagonal
passes – creating opportunities for her to isolate her
defender in 1v1 situations.
Italy, for their part, adopted a narrow shape with
two forwards. This strategy proved effective thanks to
captain Cristiana Girelli, a centre-forward capable of
receiving the ball to feet, holding it under pressure and
linking play.
From a coaching perspective, the tactical
approaches taken by Belgium’s Elisabet Gunnarsdóttir
and Italy’s Andrea Soncin offered useful lessons on how
to break down identical setups and on the ideal profile
of forward for such situations.

GRAHAM HANSEN’S 1v1

MASTERCLASS
Caroline Graham Hansen’s winning goal against Finland
followed one of the group stage’s finest examples of
1v1 play by a forward. The Norway winger cut inside
two opponents from the right touchline and, facing
Eveliina Summanen in the penalty area, she twisted
one way then the other to create the space before
chipping the ball into the net off the far post.
“She was superior in 1v1 situations in her opponents’
half,” said UEFA Technical Observer Anna Signeul.
“Even though the defender knows what she is going to
do, she has such quick feet and excellent two-footed
dribbling ability to get past them.”
The UEFA Technical Observer Group highlighted
two specific details about Graham Hansen’s dribbling:
her stop-start movements and her use of two quick
touches before beating an opponent. Defenders often
wait for a touch before tackling, but the rat-a-tat
rhythm of Graham Hansen’s two quick touches proved
a highly effective tool – including before delivering the
cross for the opening goal.

There was also strong interplay with the support she
received from her full-back, Thea Bjelde, who took up a
position inside to attract an opposition player.
An example came in the lead-up to the opening goal
when Graham Hansen cut inside past Joanna Tynnilä.
Finland’s Katariina Kosola may have been in a position
to help team-mate Tynnilä, but as the image on the
bottom left shows, she appeared caught in two minds –
looking over her shoulder at the forward run of Bjelde.
This was typical of a wider tendency seen in the
group stage, as teams like Spain and Sweden similarly
created key chances through structured wide play,
supported by movement from inside.

“I believe the plan for Italy was to exploit the space

meanwhile, was positioned wide on the right – a

opening two fixtures.

much Italy coach Andrea Soncin had looked at the
questions that both Switzerland and Finland had asked
of Norway, with their 1-3-5-2 set-ups against the
Scandinavians’ 1-4-3-3, in the group stage. It was, for

COACHING INSIGHT

MAKING CROSSING COUNT
"Effective crossing play demands the following
attributes: speed and decision-making to exploit
space; detail and variability of delivery – i.e. cutback,
flat, lofted, driven; and good movement, with the
right disguise and timing to attack the cross.
"Attacking players should have areas to target
based on where the delivery comes from and from
whom – be it a right- or left-footed player – and
there are other obvious components for a coach to
bear in mind, such as finishing, heading and blockers.
"On the training pitch, we'd focus on a range
of aspects: getting into position to cross, which
involves combination play, 1v1s, positioning;
delivery; attacking the first phase and anticipating
the second phase. On this last point, we'd anticipate
areas for delivery based on where the ball comes
from. From the touchline, you'd expect a cutback,
while if it's an early break behind the back line,
then you'd anticipate a flat or driven cross behind
the retreating defence.

And we'd predominantly
focus on always creating a scenario with a far-post
attacker due to defenders getting drawn to the front
post when ball-watching.
“As for the drills I'd use, I'd prefer to deliver small-
sided games or phases with restrictions to create
and repeat the scenarios for crossing, involving lots
of decision-making and realism.”

SPAIN’S MOVEMENT

YIELDS LATE REWARD
Germany showed impressive cohesion and resilience
in frustrating the tournament’s top scorers for 113
minutes of a compelling semi-final in Zurich. Operating
mostly in a compact 1-4-5-1 mid-block, they applied
quick, consistent pressure on the ball-carrier and made
it hard for Spain to play through them.
If challenged by Germany’s high press, Montse
Tomé’s side kept to their attacking style and, in
opposition territory, they displayed a controlled
attacking approach which bore fruit eventually with
Aitana Bonmatí’s strike.
Appraising Spain’s approach, UEFA Technical
Observer Irene Fuhrmann said: “In possession, they
always create short passing options nearby to keep
the ball moving and shift the opponent, in order to
then play vertically.
“Especially on the flanks, the full-backs frequently
overlap the midfielders to create numerical
superiority or exploit the space that has been opened
up. One tactic they often use is the third-player
combination – with an open body position and a run
behind the defensive line, they repeatedly create
dangerous situations.”

FINDING SPACE
Central to Spain’s attacking approach, added
Fuhrmann, was an individual and collective focus on
creating and exploiting space. Before her goal, for
example, Aitana could be seen scanning, standing still,
as well as adjusting her position by moving backwards,
all to create an opportunity to receive the ball in a
pocket of space.
“Spain’s players constantly scan the space around
them and, even without the ball, know how to get free
at the right moment or draw defenders away to open
up space,” explained Fuhrmann. “They create space
by circulating the ball within their own team and by
positioning themselves well in the gaps, in the spaces
between the lines, or by making dynamic runs in behind
to demand balls played beyond the defensive line.
“In addition, the Spain players are very strong in
1v1 situations. They can beat their opponents using
body feints and changes of pace when dribbling, or
they move intelligently out of their opponent’s line of
sight to find open positions between the lines.”

HOW THE GOALS WERE SCORED
The way that the goals were scored in Switzerland offered further
encouraging signs about the technical advances made in the
women’s game. With 80% of goals sourced from open play, there
was less reliance on set plays than at the 2022 tournament.
Then, 26% of the goals came via free-kicks and corners; this
time, they accounted for 12%.
“We’ve improved in terms of technical skills,” said UEFA
Technical Observer Lluís Cortés as he praised the quality of
the goals and noted the shrinking number that had come from
opposition errors.
The majority of open-play goals came against opponents
defending in a low block, with the team having to engineer a way
through, often via combination plays.

HEADERS AND FIRST-TOUCH GOALS
Although both goals in the final came from headers, there were
fewer at this year’s tournament than three years ago. There were
also fewer goals from first-touch finishes compared to in 2022. Then,
67% of goals (excluding penalties, direct-free-kicks and own goals)
came from that source while at this tournament the figure was 57%.
A decrease in the number of goals from crosses or cutbacks was a
factor in more players taking an extra touch before striking.

CHANCE CREATION

EXPLOITING A HIGH BACK LINE
The chart on the right displays each team’s total number of balls in
behind, played from between their own penalty box and the halfway
line, which led to a shot or goal.
While Netherlands were the team attempting such passes with
the most frequency (21 across their three matches), England
and Spain were the most effective at turning them into scoring
opportunities (eight each).
Five teams scored following balls in behind, with Netherlands,
Norway and England all scoring twice and Belgium and Sweden once
each. Spain did not convert any of their eight attempts created.
From a coaching perspective, the relational dimension is crucial.
Players need to be able to read the situation around the ball – if
there is pressure on the ball and if the player in possession is
facing forward, for example. Eye contact is important too, as
players require triggers.
The UEFA Technical Observer Group cited the lead-up to Victoria
Pelova’s goal for Netherlands against Wales as a noteworthy
example.

Midfield runner Danielle van de Donk’s raised arm and
movement were the trigger for the long ball from centre-back
Veerle Buurman.
“When you find the space, you need the trigger between the
passer and the receiver. It’s about the quality of the pass and of
the run,” said UEFA Technical Observer Anna Signeul, analysing the
broader trend.
Another example was Maren Mjelde’s wonderful ball behind
Italy’s defence for Ada Hegerberg’s goal in the sides’ quarter-
final. Norway had already caught the eye with the longer passing
of defenders Mjelde and Marit Bratberg Lund, which was
complemented by clever movement from players like Caroline
Graham Hansen. Her runs from ‘outside to in’ led to their second
goal in their opening fixture against Switzerland.
UEFA Technical Observer Tanya Oxtoby elaborated on Graham
Hansen’s “double movement” in that match, as she came towards
the ball before spinning behind. She explained: “Generally, as the
player in possession is having their touch and looking up, she’ll
look to come to feet.

The purpose is to drag the defender with her,
knowing full well that she’s actually looking to exploit the space
in behind.”

BREAKING DOWN A LOW BLOCK
Engineering 1v1 situations
Delphine Cascarino’s Goal of the Tournament for France against
the Netherlands, perfectly showcases a player utilising individual
skill to beat an opponent and create the space to shoot.
Yet, as this tournament showed, there are also structural
tactics teams can use to engineer 1v1 situations and enable their
individual talents to shine. For example, in their group win over
Poland, Germany pushed both full-backs into advanced positions
during the first half. In contrast, after the break, they remained
deeper for longer, which kept the Poland wingers higher, creating
more space and 1v1 possibilities for their own wingers – as
depicted in the image below of Klara Bühl on the attack.
In the opening 15 minutes, the average distance between left-
back Sarai Linder and winger Bühl was 7.8m. This then decreased
to 5m in the following 15 minutes. In the second half, the distance
between the pair increased to 13.3m.

By full-time, Bühl had produced ten take-ons in the opposition
half, the most in the match, with fellow winger Brand ranked
second with four. As the graphic on the right displays, on Matchday
1, the pair led the way for take-ons and dribbles combined. Their
shared output included four ball carries, each leading to a shot –
one of which brought Brand’s goal.
Summing up Bühl’s 1v1 threat, UEFA Technical Observer Anna
Signeul said: “By starting wide, Klara aims to find the space needed
to accelerate past the defender and beat her on the outside.
“She’s also versatile. She can go on the inside and outside, with a
change of pace. She can drive the ball with speed and keep it close
to her feet to protect it. Her ability to pass, cross and shoot with
both feet is a huge advantage, as it makes it difficult for a defender
to direct her.”

Oxtoby said: “I always talk about exploiting or creating space.
Diani here uses her pace and power to be a decoy runner, creating
space for her team-mates by running through opposition eyelines
and affecting their decision-making.
“The runner may not be looking to receive the ball themselves;
instead, their movement can create space for someone else.

In this
way, France disrupted Wales’ ability to stay in the block, detaching
the full-backs from their centre-backs in order to exploit the space
between with clever combinations.”

COACHING INSIGHT
COACHING 1v1 ATTACKING
“Every coach wants difference-makers. But you only find
that kind of player by not dictating everything in training and
allowing them to experiment,” explains Irene Fuhrmann. “The
goal should be to develop confident, creative players who can
solve problems under pressure.
“The first step is to learn dribbling moves and feints in space.
Then, to progress from the technical aspects to decision-
making under pressure, I’d focus on small-sided games. That
way, players are constantly tested in one-on-one situations
with little space and lots of pressure, and will constantly need
to find solutions. Ultimately, don’t overcoach – instead, ask
players questions and encourage self-reflection.”

tracked consistently.”

FRANCE OVERLOADS
Although they were beaten 4-1 eventually, Wales performed
well defensively in the first half of their fixture against France.
Defending in a 1-4-4-2, they had both their forwards and central
midfield players working effectively at stopping inside passes from
wide areas.
As UEFA Technical Observer Tanya Oxtoby said: “They were
patient and happy for France to switch play at the back, protecting
central areas, but the moment the ball was played into wide areas,
they looked to shut off passing lanes inside the pitch, particularly to   support the
the inner corridor.”
To achieve this, they looked for defensive overloads – or, at the
very least, parity in numbers. When France brought an extra player
across to support the attack, Wales would do the same, often with
a central midfield player coming across to support the winger and
full-back in a 3v3.

As a result, France found it difficult to find players in the pocket
and, as Oxtoby added, this led to a change of approach in the second
half – offering an example of how to undo opponents in a mid-block.
“France occupied space between the lines better in the second
half. What that did was to narrow off Wales, which then let France
try to exploit the wide areas where they were good in 1v1 situations.
They managed to detach the Wales full-backs from their centre-
backs and exploit the space between with clever combinations.”

In a tournament of just 11 clean sheets, teams defending deep
typically kept their opponents out for only so long.
That said, UEFA’s Technical Observer Group identified several
strong case studies, starting with how Germany defended against
France with ten players from the 13th minute to the end of extra
time, after Kathrin Hendrich’s dismissal. Save for Grace Geyoro’s
15th-minute penalty, they managed to frustrate France and take
the game to penalties, despite just 27% of possession.
Defending in the 1-4-4-1 structure, Christian Wück’s team
tried to keep their back line high where possible, with goalkeeper
Ann-Katrin Berger playing a central role organising from the back.
When France’s centre-backs had the ball, she positioned herself
high outside the box ready to react to any through balls in behind.
As for the defenders, they were ready to drop to protect the
space behind when needed, or to stay connected to the midfield
to defend passes in between. UEFA Technical Observer Irene
Fuhrmann added: “They shifted together to keep the spaces
between players tight.

This allowed them to block passing lanes
into the centre and repeatedly force the French players into
passing backwards and switches of play, through which Germany
could prevent vertical breakthroughs and buy valuable time.
“Although Germany had one player less, they still managed to
create equality, if not even superiority, in the wide areas. Germany
didn’t allow themselves to be pulled out of position by France’s
positional rotations. They handed over or took over players moving
into their zones. The wide midfielders were always ready to support
their full-backs.”

PROACTIVE APPROACH TO

PREVENTING CHANCES
Every goalkeeper’s actions are influenced by factors such as
playing style, playing system and game strategy. For example,
if her team are defending in a low block, this will mean more
interventions in her own penalty area. If they are pressing high, the
goalkeeper has to protect the space behind the defensive line, so
the interventions are outside, close to or inside the penalty area.
As a broad trend, female goalkeepers have become more
proactive and the UEFA Goalkeeper Experts cited the example of
Spain’s Cata Coll against Germany.
The first image on the right captures the moment that Coll got
to the ball, just ahead of Giovanna Hoffmann, her good positional
play having enabled her to make a positive decision to come out
and deal with a long ball down the Germany right.
According to the UEFA Goalkeeper Expert Group: “Most of
the goalkeepers adapted to playing in a high position and were
proactive in and out of possession so we can observe progress
in this area.

During the tournament we saw several interesting
interventions outside the box with a pass to a team-mate or
clearing behind the line.”
Inside the penalty box, they saw impressive interventions too,
such as the example of Iceland’s Cecilía Rúnarsdóttir diving at the
feet of a Norway forward in 1v1 situation.
“Mentally the goalkeepers showed a lot of courage,” they
elaborated. “Physically, more explosiveness and agility allowed
for more dynamic interventions. Game-reading and decision-
making are crucial for the goalkeeper to understand what kind
of intervention to use in these situations.” The same applied in
open-play crossing situations, such as when Sweden’s Jennifer
Falk defended a cross against England – as shown in the third
image on the right.
“She was in a high position, shaping to step out, at the moment
of the delivery and this allowed her be in the right place, close to
the penalty spot, to get to the ball first and punch away,” said the
UEFA Goalkeeper Experts.

The final image is another example highlighted, this time from
a set play, with Poland’s Kinga Szemik getting through a crowd of
players to catch a cross and immediately launching a quick attack
with a long throw.

CHALLENGE OF DEALING

WITH CROSSING VARIETY
The UEFA Goalkeeper Experts felt that, across the tournament,
goalkeepers dealt well with crosses to the near post and to the
middle of the goal as well as with low crosses. On the flipside,
cutbacks presented difficulties at times, as did crosses to the far
post. “The accuracy and the speed of these balls are much higher,
which makes the situation for the goalkeepers more complicated,”
they remarked on the challenge of far-post crosses.
As for cutbacks, they said: “With balls coming in front of the
goal, between the byline and goalkeeper’s box line – or the byline
and closest defender – their position in the goal and set position
didn’t allow them to dive and intercept the ball. The goalkeepers
are thinking much more about the second ball. We think this needs
deeper analysis.”
POSITIVE GOALKEEPERS RISE

TO SET-PLAY CHALLENGE
When it came to defending set plays, the goalkeeping was positive
in the eyes of the UEFA Goalkeeper Experts. “Today’s goalkeepers
are more proactive and robust,” they said. “It is not only their
height and significantly improved athleticism that play a decisive
role, but also their ability to assess high balls, defend them with the
appropriate technical skills and act without compromise.”
The evidence of the tournament was that goalkeepers are more
active in seeking out and winning duels, and in using the punch
more. The example below of Switzerland goalkeeper Livia Peng
gathering a Norway free-kick offers a case in point. “She adjusts
her position slightly before the free-kick is taken, then attacks
the long ball with determination and does not allow herself to be
affected by direct physical contact with the opponent,” they said.

FITNESS
The UEFA Fitness Group put the teams’ physical data under
the microscope, with high-intensity output up significantly and
some marked variations according to position and tactics
Towards the end of her press conference after England’s final
victory, Sarina Wiegman began a reflection that went beyond
her own team’s exploits to touch on broader tournament
trends. And it was telling that she soon landed on the physical
aspect of the matches in Switzerland, declaring: “The intensity
of the games went through the roof.”
That assertion from the winning coach of the last three
Women’s EUROs aligned with the view of the UEFA Technical
Observer Group, with Anna Signeul highlighting this aspect
when she said: “I’ve been immensely impressed by the
intensity of the games and the fitness level of the players. In
the three years since the previous EURO, the fitness level has
increased very much.”
Intensity is the apposite word. The average total distance
covered per player at this tournament was actually lower
than in 2022 yet high-intensity output increased.

By way
of example, the average distance covered by wingers when
running at high speed in Switzerland was 799m per game,
compared to 588m in 2022. In other words, wingers sprinted
200m more per game on average than they had done at the
previous Women’s EURO.
Another example comes from the players in the midfield
pivot/No6 position whose average distance covered
increased by 1.3km per game to 10.8km – the highest output
of any position.

COACHING DRILLS
BUILDING FROM

THE BACK
Session organisation
• 20 players + 2 goalkeepers
• Orange team always start with the ball from goal kick
• Yellow team to advance the ball and attack with numerical
advantage (5 vs 4 + Goalkeeper)
• Purple team to regain the ball and counter towards the
opposite goal
88
UEFA WOMEN’S EURO 2025 | T E C H N I C A L R E P O R T

Coaching points
• Attract the pressure and then find free player to connect over
the first lines of press
• Third-man combination: support vs deep moves
• Create advantages that can be used to play forward
• Create overloads from behind: be proactive
• Play under pressure
• Vertical moves after winning the advantage
THIRD-PLAYER

COMBINATIONS
Session organisation
• 19 players total: 9 attackers + GK (Orange), 7 defenders + GK (Purple)
and 1 neutral player (always supports team in possession)
• Set up a pitch divided into three vertical zones (A–B–C)
• The Orange team (9 players) always start in possession
• Neutral player supports the team in possession and can move freely
across zones
• Rules for Orange (in possession):
- If the ball travels from Zone A to Zone B, the players in Zone B must
return the ball to Zone A (to attract pressure)
- If the ball goes directly from Zone A to Zone C, players in Zone C must
combine with a third-player action via Zone B before freely attacking
- Once a third-player combination is achieved through Zone B, Zone B
players can join the attack into Zone C
• Rules for Purple (out of possession):
- Defenders can move freely across all zones
- Upon regaining possession, their objective is to counterattack
and score as quickly as possible

Coaching points
• Third-player combinations: Emphasise using central
players (Zone B) as links to break lines and commit
opponents
• Attract and release: Use Zone B intentionally to
draw defenders out of position before switching or
advancing
• Neutral player’s role: Provide support between lines
to maintain circulation and enable combination play
• Defensive transition: Encourage quick reactions on
loss of possession — nearest player applies pressure,
others cover and delay
89
COACHING DRILLS
WIDE PLAY

AND OVERLOAD
Session organisation
• 10 + 6 + 1 Goalkeeper
• Orange team always start with the ball
• Must switch the play from one side to the other before attacking
– they can switch multiple times if needed
• Purples start on edge of box and can defend “live”
• Oranges have to score from a cutback or ball played back to half-
space outside the box + cross
90
UEFA WOMEN’S EURO 2025 | T E C H N I C A L R E P O R T

Coaching points
• Side pocket players must run in behind full-back
• Choice for wide players is to play the ball for the deep run or play
the ball backwards to the edge player
• If the player tracks the run of the player in behind and the cross
is blocked – option to play back to edge player to cross from half-
space outside the box
• Details on crossing to beat first defender
• Timing of runs from opposite side in between gaps
• Second balls: rest defence to maintain the attack
DEFENSIVE

COMPACTNESS
Session organisation
Coaching points
• 19 players + 1 goalkeeper
• Pressing triggers within the block: when and where to
press, forcing backwards
• Orange team build from the back and aim to progress
through the pitch
• Defending concepts: body position, orientation,
aggressiveness, distances
• Orange team score by finishing in the big goal
• Lines coordination: press, cover and balance, closing
• Purple team defend in mid-block
central lanes
• When Purple team regain the ball, they can score
• Offensive transition: speed and quality of execution
in either of the three mini goals
